subject: technology-sp
description: Technology Senior Phase (Grades 7–9) question bank. One 20-item pool per atomic skill (the topic key IS the skill id). Content subject: 0.6 pass mark, mastery via lib/content-mastery.ts. Tap-only; no free text.

TECH.G7.DG.A1.title: What is Technology?
TECH.G7.DG.A1.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G7 T1) — Design process & graphics: What is Technology?.
TECH.G7.DG.A1.recovery_strategy: Technology means using knowledge, skills and resources to solve people's real problems.

questions.question: What does Technology mean as a school subject?
options: Using knowledge and skills to solve people's real problems
questions.expected: Using knowledge and skills to solve people's real problems
questions.memo: Technology means using knowledge, skills, values and resources to solve people's needs and wants with practical solutions.

questions.question: Technology is about solving real problems for people, not just memorising facts.
questions.memo: Technology is a 'doing' subject — it uses knowledge to build practical solutions to real needs and wants.

questions.question: Which of these is the BEST example of technology solving a need?
options: Designing a cheap water filter for a village
questions.expected: Designing a cheap water filter for a village
questions.memo: Technology meets a real need (clean water) with a practical solution — that is exactly what the subject is about.

questions.question: Technology uses knowledge, skills and resources to meet people's needs and ____.
questions.memo: Technology develops practical solutions to people's needs AND wants.

questions.question: Which job uses technology and design every day?
options: A civil engineer designing a bridge
questions.expected: A civil engineer designing a bridge
questions.memo: Engineers, architects and technicians all use the design process to solve problems — these are technology careers.

questions.question: Engineers, architects and electricians are all careers that use technology.
questions.memo: Technology introduces learners to careers like civil, mechanical and electrical engineering and architecture.

questions.question: Why was Technology added to the school curriculum?
options: To build a technologically literate population and future engineers and artisans
To give learners less to do
questions.expected: To build a technologically literate population and future engineers and artisans
questions.memo: Technology was introduced to produce engineers, technicians and artisans, and a technologically literate society.

questions.question: A person who designs and builds machines is a ____ engineer.
questions.memo: Mechanical engineers design machines; civil engineers design structures; electrical engineers design wiring.

questions.question: Technology asks us to think about society and the environment when we design. Why?
options: Our solutions affect people and the planet
questions.expected: Our solutions affect people and the planet
questions.memo: Good technology weighs the impact on society and the environment — solutions must not harm people or the planet.

questions.question: In Technology you must be able to USE knowledge, not just remember it.
questions.memo: Knowledge matters, but Technology assesses whether you can apply it to solve a problem.

questions.question: Which skill is NOT a main part of technology?
questions.memo: Technology uses investigating, designing, making, evaluating and communicating — not random guessing.

questions.question: A 'technologically literate' person is someone who can…
options: understand and use technology sensibly in daily life
questions.expected: understand and use technology sensibly in daily life
questions.memo: Technological literacy means being able to understand, use and judge technology in everyday life.

questions.question: Technology helps prepare learners to make ____ choices at the end of Grade 9.
questions.memo: Technology gives learners experience that helps them choose FET subjects and careers at the end of Grade 9.

questions.question: Technology only happens inside a classroom and never in the real world.
questions.memo: Technology uses authentic, real-world contexts — problems from outside the classroom.

questions.question: Which is a 'want' rather than a 'need'?
questions.memo: Needs are things we must have to live (water, food, shelter); wants make life nicer but are not essential.

questions.question: An artisan is best described as…
options: a skilled worker who makes or fixes things by hand
questions.expected: a skilled worker who makes or fixes things by hand
questions.memo: Artisans are skilled trades-people (like welders or electricians) — a key technology career path.

questions.question: Technology develops creative and critical thinking and teamwork.
questions.memo: The subject builds creative thinking, problem solving, time and resource management, and teamwork.

questions.question: Designing the electrical wiring for a lamp is the work of an ____.
questions.memo: An electrician designs and installs electrical wiring — an electrical-technology career.

questions.question: Sort each activity into 'Technology' or 'Not technology'.

items.text: Building a model crane to lift a load

questions.expected: Designing a desk and building a crane solve real problems (technology); daydreaming and reciting do not.
questions.memo: Technology means solving a real problem with a practical solution — making and designing, not just remembering.

questions.question: The best short definition of technology is using resources to…
questions.memo: Technology = using knowledge, skills and resources to solve problems and meet people's needs and wants.

TECH.G7.DG.A2.title: The design process (IDMEC)
TECH.G7.DG.A2.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G7 T1) — Design process & graphics: The design process (IDMEC).
TECH.G7.DG.A2.recovery_strategy: The design process: Investigate, Design, Make, Evaluate, Communicate.

questions.question: What do the letters in the design process IDMEC stand for?
questions.memo: The design process is Investigate, Design, Make, Evaluate, Communicate — the backbone of Technology.

questions.question: The design process is the steps we follow to develop a solution to a problem.
questions.memo: The design process is a systematic way of moving from a problem to a working solution.

questions.question: In which stage do you find out about the problem and existing products?
questions.memo: Investigating means finding out about the context, the need, and existing products.

questions.question: In which stage do you write a design brief and sketch ideas?
questions.memo: Designing includes writing the design brief and specifications and sketching initial ideas.

questions.question: In which stage do you actually build the model or product?
questions.memo: Making is where you draw working plans and build the item or model.

questions.question: What happens in the Evaluate stage?
options: You judge how well the solution works against the brief
questions.expected: You judge how well the solution works against the brief
questions.memo: Evaluating means checking your design and product against the design brief and criteria.

questions.question: What is the Communicate stage about?
options: Presenting and recording your solution with drawings and notes
questions.expected: Presenting and recording your solution with drawings and notes
questions.memo: Communicating means presenting your solution and recording it in drawings and a report.

questions.question: A short written statement of what you must design is called a design ____.
questions.memo: The design brief states the problem and what the solution must do.

questions.question: Specifications are the exact requirements the solution must meet.
questions.memo: Specifications spell out the requirements (size, cost, materials, safety) the solution must satisfy.

questions.question: Limits you must work within, like cost or time, are called ____.
questions.memo: Constraints are the limits — money, time, materials — that you must work within.

questions.question: The design process must always be followed in a strict one-way order and you may never go back.
questions.memo: The design process is non-linear — you can investigate or evaluate at any point and go back to improve a design.

questions.question: You build your model and find a part is too weak, so you change the design. This shows the process is…
options: non-linear — you can go back and improve
questions.expected: non-linear — you can go back and improve
questions.memo: Going back to improve a design when you hit a problem is normal — the process is non-linear.

questions.question: Which comes first for a brand-new problem?
questions.memo: You begin by investigating the problem, need or opportunity before designing.

questions.question: Choosing the best idea from several sketches uses your ____ skills.
questions.memo: Evaluation skills are used to compare ideas and choose the best one.

questions.question: Put the design process stages in their usual order.

items.text: Design ideas and choose the best

questions.memo: The usual order is Investigate, Design, Make, Evaluate, Communicate — though you may loop back at any time.

questions.question: Sort each task into the correct design-process stage.

items.text: Look at how existing desks are built
Sketch two ideas for a new desk
Cut and join the parts to build the desk

questions.expected: Looking at existing desks is investigating; sketching and writing the brief are designing; cutting and joining is making.
questions.memo: Each task belongs to a stage: investigate (find out), design (plan/sketch), make (build).

questions.question: Investigating can only happen at the very start and never again.
questions.memo: Investigation can happen at any point in the design process, not only at the beginning.

questions.question: Why is the Communicate stage important?
options: So others understand and can use your solution
questions.expected: So others understand and can use your solution
questions.memo: Communicating shares the solution clearly so a client or class understands it.

questions.question: The design process is the 'backbone' of Technology because…
options: it structures how every task is tackled
questions.expected: it structures how every task is tackled
questions.memo: Every Technology task is structured around the design process from start to finish.

questions.question: A learner keeps changing a design after testing each version. This shows the design process is…
questions.memo: Designing is iterative — you test, evaluate and improve again and again.

TECH.G7.DG.A3.title: Design considerations & fitness-for-purpose
TECH.G7.DG.A3.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G7 T1) — Design process & graphics: Design considerations & fitness-for-purpose.
TECH.G7.DG.A3.recovery_strategy: Fit-for-purpose asks: who is it for, will it do the job, is it safe, does it look good?

questions.question: 'Fitness-for-purpose' asks one key question. Which is it?
options: Will it do the job it was made for?
questions.expected: Will it do the job it was made for?
questions.memo: Fit-for-purpose means the product actually does the job it was designed to do.

questions.question: What does 'ergonomics' consider in a design?
options: How easy and comfortable it is for people to use
questions.expected: How easy and comfortable it is for people to use
questions.memo: Ergonomics is about how comfortable and easy a product is to use for people.

questions.question: What does 'aesthetics' mean when judging a design?
questions.memo: Aesthetics is about how attractive or good-looking a product is.

questions.question: A safe design is an important design consideration.
questions.memo: Safety is a key design criterion — a product must be safe to make and to use.

questions.question: Getting good value for the money spent is called cost ____.
questions.memo: Cost-effectiveness (value for money) means the product is worth what it costs.

questions.question: A wheelchair ramp is judged 'fit-for-purpose' if it…
options: lets a wheelchair user get up safely and easily
questions.expected: lets a wheelchair user get up safely and easily
questions.memo: Fit-for-purpose means it does its job — here, letting a wheelchair user get up safely.

questions.question: A beautiful product that does not do its job is still a good design.
questions.memo: If a product does not do its job it is NOT fit-for-purpose, no matter how good it looks.

questions.question: Which question is about environmental impact?
questions.memo: Environmental impact asks whether the product harms or helps the environment.

questions.question: Designs should be checked against set requirements, called the design ____.
questions.memo: Design criteria are the points a design is checked against (cost, safety, looks, etc.).

questions.question: Who should a designer think about first?
options: The user the product is for
questions.expected: The user the product is for
questions.memo: Good design starts with the user — who is it for and what do they need?

questions.question: Which is a sign of poor ergonomics?
options: A handle too small and sharp to hold comfortably
questions.expected: A handle too small and sharp to hold comfortably
questions.memo: Poor ergonomics makes a product uncomfortable or hard to use, like a sharp, tiny handle.

questions.question: Designers should think about whether a product could unfairly disadvantage a group of people.
questions.memo: Good design considers bias — whether a product favours or disadvantages certain groups.

questions.question: How easy a product is to manufacture is called ease of ____.
questions.memo: Ease of manufacture is a design criterion — can it be made simply and cheaply?

questions.question: A torch designed for elderly users should mainly be…
options: easy to grip and switch on
questions.expected: easy to grip and switch on
questions.memo: Designing for the user (the elderly) means easy grip and simple switching — good ergonomics.

questions.question: Match each design word to what it checks. Sort them into the right group.
questions.expected: Aesthetics is about looks; ergonomics and safety are about using it; cost-effectiveness is about money.
questions.memo: Aesthetics = looks; ergonomics & safety = using it; cost-effectiveness = value for money.

questions.question: Fitness-for-purpose means the product suits the job it was designed for.
questions.memo: Fit-for-purpose = the product is suitable for, and does, its intended job.

questions.question: Which design would be the most fit-for-purpose for carrying hot food?
options: An insulated container with a tight lid
questions.expected: An insulated container with a tight lid
questions.memo: Fit-for-purpose for hot food means keeping heat in and not spilling — an insulated sealed container.

questions.question: Why consider cost when designing?
options: So the user can afford it and it gives value
To make it as expensive as possible
questions.expected: So the user can afford it and it gives value
questions.memo: Cost matters so the product is affordable and offers value for money.

questions.question: A product that is comfortable and easy to use has good ____.
questions.memo: Good ergonomics means a product fits the user comfortably and is easy to use.

questions.question: A design that is dangerous to use should be improved, even if it looks good.
questions.memo: Safety outranks looks — an unsafe design must be improved before it is acceptable.

TECH.G7.DG.A4.title: Graphical communication & line types
TECH.G7.DG.A4.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G7 T1) — Design process & graphics: Graphical communication & line types.
TECH.G7.DG.A4.recovery_strategy: Drawings use different lines: dark outlines, feint construction lines and dashed hidden detail.

questions.question: Why do we use drawings in Technology?
options: To develop ideas and communicate them clearly
questions.expected: To develop ideas and communicate them clearly
questions.memo: Graphics serve two purposes: developing ideas and communicating them to others.

questions.question: How are the visible outlines of an object usually drawn?
questions.memo: Outlines (the visible edges) are drawn as thick, dark, solid lines.

questions.question: How is hidden detail (an edge you cannot see) shown on a drawing?
questions.memo: Hidden detail is drawn with dashed lines to show edges that are behind the object.

questions.question: What are construction lines used for?
options: Light guide lines to help build the drawing
questions.expected: Light guide lines to help build the drawing
questions.memo: Construction lines are thin and feint — light guide lines you draw first to position things.

questions.question: Construction lines should be drawn thin and feint (light).
questions.memo: Construction lines are feint guide lines, drawn lightly so they don't clutter the final drawing.

questions.question: Numbers on a drawing that show the size of parts are called ____.
questions.memo: Dimensions are the measurements written on a drawing to show sizes.

questions.question: What does 'scale' mean on a drawing?
options: The drawing is a set number of times bigger or smaller than the real object
questions.expected: The drawing is a set number of times bigger or smaller than the real object
questions.memo: Scale relates the size of the drawing to the real object (e.g. 1:2 means half size).

questions.question: A free-hand sketch is drawn quickly without using a ruler.
questions.memo: Free-hand sketching is done quickly by hand, without instruments, to capture ideas.

questions.question: A working drawing of one face of an object is drawn in…
questions.memo: A working drawing of one face is a flat, 2D drawing using conventions and dimensions.

questions.question: Visible edges of an object are drawn as thick, ____ lines.
questions.memo: Outlines are thick and dark; construction lines are thin and feint; hidden detail is dashed.

questions.question: Which line type would show the edge of a hole drilled through the back of a block (not visible from the front)?
questions.memo: An edge you cannot see is hidden detail, shown with a dashed line.

questions.question: Drawing conventions are agreed rules so everyone reads a drawing the same way.
questions.memo: Conventions are shared rules (line types, dimensions, scale) so any reader understands the drawing.

questions.question: Why write dimensions on a working drawing?
options: So the maker knows the exact sizes to build
questions.expected: So the maker knows the exact sizes to build
questions.memo: Dimensions tell the maker the exact sizes needed to build the object.

questions.question: Drawing something half its real size uses a scale of 1 to ____.
questions.memo: A scale of 1:2 means the drawing is half the size of the real object.

questions.question: Match each line use to the correct line type.

items.text: A light guide line used while drawing
An edge hidden behind the object

questions.expected: Visible edges and the final shape are thick/dark; guide lines are thin/feint; hidden edges are dashed.
questions.memo: Thick/dark = visible edges; thin/feint = construction guides; dashed = hidden detail.

questions.question: Two main reasons we draw in Technology are to develop ideas and to…
questions.memo: Graphics develop ideas in your head and communicate them clearly to others.

questions.question: Scale lets you draw a large object, like a tower, on a small piece of paper.
questions.memo: Scaling down lets big objects be drawn to fit on paper while keeping the proportions correct.

questions.question: Which is drawn first when starting a careful drawing?
questions.memo: You start with feint construction lines to position the drawing, then darken the final outlines.

questions.question: Hidden edges of an object are shown using ____ lines.
questions.memo: Dashed lines show hidden detail — edges that are there but not visible.

questions.question: A drawing is labelled 'scale 1:5'. This means the real object is…
questions.memo: Scale 1:5 means 1 unit on the drawing equals 5 units on the real object — the object is 5× bigger.

TECH.G7.DG.A5.title: Drawing techniques: sketch, oblique, perspective
TECH.G7.DG.A5.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G7 T1) — Design process & graphics: Drawing techniques: sketch, oblique, perspective.
TECH.G7.DG.A5.recovery_strategy: Sketches, flat working drawings and 3D drawings each show an object a different way.

questions.question: In 3D oblique drawing, the front face is drawn true shape and the depth lines go back at…
questions.memo: Oblique drawing shows the front face true, with depth lines going back at 45°.

questions.question: Which drawing technique makes things look smaller as they go into the distance, meeting at one point?
questions.memo: Single-point perspective uses one vanishing point so things shrink into the distance.

questions.question: A working drawing shows exact sizes and is used to build the object.
questions.memo: Working drawings carry dimensions and conventions so the object can be built accurately.

questions.question: Which technique is best for quickly capturing a first idea?
questions.memo: Free-hand sketching is the fast way to get early ideas down on paper.

questions.question: Oblique and perspective are both ways of drawing in ____.
questions.memo: Oblique and perspective are 3D drawing techniques; a working drawing of one face is 2D.

questions.question: A single vanishing point perspective drawing usually has…
options: one point where lines meet in the distance
questions.expected: one point where lines meet in the distance
questions.memo: Single-point perspective has exactly one vanishing point.

questions.question: Oblique drawings are often done on squared (quadrant) paper to help keep the 45° depth.
questions.memo: Squared paper helps draw the 45° depth lines neatly in oblique projection.

questions.question: Which is a 2D drawing?
options: A flat working drawing of one face
questions.expected: A flat working drawing of one face
questions.memo: A working drawing of a single face is two-dimensional (flat).

questions.question: Adding colour, texture and shading helps a drawing look more ____.
questions.memo: Artistic techniques like colour, texture and shading make a drawing look realistic.

questions.question: Which drawing would you give to someone to BUILD the object accurately?
questions.memo: The dimensioned working drawing is the one used to build accurately.

questions.question: An artistic impression is mainly used to communicate how the finished product will look.
questions.memo: Artistic impressions (perspective, colour, shading) communicate the look of the final product.

questions.question: Free-hand sketching is best described as…
options: drawing quickly by hand without instruments
questions.expected: drawing quickly by hand without instruments
questions.memo: Free-hand sketching is fast hand drawing without rulers or instruments.

questions.question: In oblique drawing the depth lines go back at ____ degrees.
questions.memo: Oblique projection uses 45° for the depth lines.

questions.question: Match each drawing type to its best use.
questions.expected: Sketches capture ideas, working drawings are for building, artistic impressions show the final look.
questions.memo: Sketch = fast ideas; working drawing = accurate building; artistic impression = final appearance.

TECH.G7.ST.A1.title: Purpose & classification of structures
TECH.G7.ST.A1.description: Structures (CAPS G7 T2) — Structures: Purpose & classification of structures.
TECH.G7.ST.A1.recovery_strategy: A structure contains, supports, protects or spans; it can be natural or man-made.

questions.question: What is a structure?
options: Something built to support a load or hold things together
questions.expected: Something built to support a load or hold things together
questions.memo: A structure supports a load and holds its shape — it can contain, support, protect or span.

questions.question: Which is a job a structure can do?
options: Span a gap, like a bridge
questions.expected: Span a gap, like a bridge
questions.memo: Structures contain, support, protect or span. A bridge spans a gap.

questions.question: A dam wall mainly works to…
questions.memo: A dam wall is a structure that contains (holds back) water.

questions.question: Which is a NATURAL structure?
questions.memo: Natural structures are made by nature (webs, nests, bones); man-made structures are built by people.

questions.question: Which is a MAN-MADE structure?
questions.memo: Man-made structures are built by people, like towers and bridges.

questions.question: A bird's nest is an example of a natural structure.
questions.memo: A nest is built by an animal from natural materials — a natural structure.

questions.question: A helmet is a structure that works to ____ your head.
questions.memo: A helmet protects — one of the jobs of a structure.

questions.question: All structures are made by people.
questions.memo: Many structures are natural (webs, bones, shells); only some are man-made.

questions.question: A roof beam mainly works to…
questions.memo: A beam supports the load above it — supporting is a key structural job.

questions.question: Bridges are structures that ____ a gap.
questions.memo: Spanning means reaching across a gap — what a bridge does.

questions.question: Which list shows only structures?
questions.memo: Bridges, towers and houses are all structures; water, music and ideas are not.

questions.question: A human skeleton is a natural structure that supports the body.
questions.memo: Bones form a natural structure that supports and protects the body.

questions.question: A fence around a garden mainly works to…
questions.memo: A fence encloses and protects an area — a structural job.

questions.question: Structures built by people are called ____ structures.
questions.memo: Man-made structures are built by people; natural ones occur in nature.

questions.question: Sort each structure into 'Natural' or 'Man-made'.
questions.expected: Webs and honeycomb are natural; bridges and towers are man-made.
questions.memo: Natural structures are made by nature; man-made structures are built by people.

questions.question: Sort each structure by the main job it does.
questions.expected: A truss and table legs support; a water tank contains; a footbridge spans.
questions.memo: Structures can support a load, contain something, protect, or span a gap.

questions.question: Which best lists the jobs a structure can do?
questions.memo: The four structural jobs are to contain, support, protect and span.

questions.question: A tortoise shell is a natural structure that protects the animal.
questions.memo: The shell is a natural protective structure.

questions.question: A grain silo is a structure that mainly…
questions.memo: A silo contains and stores grain — a containing structure.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a job that structures do?
questions.memo: Structures contain, support, protect or span — generating electricity is not a structural job.

TECH.G7.ST.A2.title: Types of structures: shell, frame, solid
TECH.G7.ST.A2.description: Structures (CAPS G7 T2) — Structures: Types of structures: shell, frame, solid.
TECH.G7.ST.A2.recovery_strategy: Three structure types: shell (hollow), frame (bars joined) and solid (one mass).

questions.question: What are the three main types of structures?
questions.memo: The three structure types are shell, frame and solid.

questions.question: A frame structure is made of…
questions.memo: A frame structure is built from bars (members) joined together, like a tower or truss.

questions.question: A shell structure is best described as…
questions.memo: A shell structure is a thin hollow form, like an egg, a dome or a drink can.

questions.question: A solid structure is…
options: made from one solid mass of material
questions.expected: made from one solid mass of material
questions.memo: A solid structure is one full mass, like a brick wall or a dam wall.

questions.question: Which is a frame structure?
questions.memo: A pylon is built from joined bars — a frame structure.

questions.question: Which is a shell structure?
questions.memo: A drink can is a thin hollow covering — a shell structure.

questions.question: Which is a solid structure?
questions.memo: A dam wall is one solid mass — a solid structure.

questions.question: An egg is an example of a shell structure.
questions.memo: An egg is a thin hollow covering — a natural shell structure.

questions.question: A bicycle frame is a frame structure made of joined tubes.
questions.memo: A bicycle frame is built from joined tubes (members) — a frame structure.

questions.question: A structure made of a thin, hollow skin is a ____ structure.
questions.memo: Shell structures are thin and hollow, like cans, domes and eggs.

questions.question: A structure built from bars joined together is a ____ structure.
questions.memo: Frame structures use joined bars (members), like towers and trusses.

questions.question: Why might a frame structure use less material than a solid one of the same size?
options: It is mostly open space between the bars
questions.expected: It is mostly open space between the bars
questions.memo: Frames are mostly open, so they use less material while still being strong.

questions.question: A dome over a stadium is a shell structure.
questions.memo: A thin curved dome covering a space is a shell structure.

questions.question: Which structure type is a high-voltage tower most likely to be?
questions.memo: Pylons/towers are frame structures built of joined steel members.

questions.question: Sort each object into shell, frame or solid.
questions.expected: Tin can and egg are shells; pylon and truss are frames; a brick is solid.
questions.memo: Shell = thin hollow skin; frame = joined bars; solid = one full mass.

questions.question: A solid structure is always hollow inside.
questions.memo: A solid structure is one full mass — it is NOT hollow. Hollow thin forms are shells.

questions.question: A worksheet asks you to classify a wire bird cage. It is a…
questions.memo: A bird cage is made of joined wire bars — a frame structure.

questions.question: Which pair are both shell structures?
options: A helmet and a drink can
questions.expected: A helmet and a drink can
questions.memo: A helmet and a can are both thin hollow coverings — shell structures.

questions.question: A brick wall is an example of a ____ structure.
questions.memo: A brick wall is one solid mass — a solid structure.

questions.question: A car body that is a thin hollow shell is an example of a shell structure.
questions.memo: A car body is a thin hollow outer covering — a shell structure.

TECH.G7.ST.A3.title: Stiffening & reinforcing
TECH.G7.ST.A3.description: Structures (CAPS G7 T2) — Structures: Stiffening & reinforcing.
TECH.G7.ST.A3.recovery_strategy: You can stiffen materials by folding, rolling into tubes, or triangulating a frame.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'stiffen' a material?
questions.memo: Stiffening makes a material more rigid — harder to bend or flex.

questions.question: Folding a flat sheet of paper into a fan shape makes it…
questions.memo: Folding (corrugating) a sheet stiffens it so it resists bending.

questions.question: Rolling a sheet of paper into a tube makes it…
options: stronger and stiffer than the flat sheet
questions.expected: stronger and stiffer than the flat sheet
questions.memo: Rolling paper into a tube greatly stiffens it — tubing is a reinforcing method.

questions.question: What is triangulation in a structure?
options: Adding diagonal members to form triangles for rigidity
questions.expected: Adding diagonal members to form triangles for rigidity
questions.memo: Triangulation adds diagonals to make triangles, which keep a frame rigid.

questions.question: A triangle is a very rigid shape used to stiffen frame structures.
questions.memo: Triangles do not deform under load, so triangulating a frame stiffens it.

questions.question: A square frame is more rigid than a triangulated frame.
questions.memo: A plain square can rack (lean over); adding a diagonal to triangulate it makes it rigid.

questions.question: Adding diagonals to make triangles in a frame is called ____.
questions.memo: Triangulation = adding diagonal members so the frame is full of rigid triangles.

questions.question: A bookshelf sags in the middle under heavy books. Best way to stiffen it?
options: Add a support or a folded edge to the shelf
questions.expected: Add a support or a folded edge to the shelf
questions.memo: A support or a folded/upturned edge stiffens the shelf so it stops sagging.

questions.question: Corrugated cardboard is strong for its weight because…
options: the wavy folded layer stiffens it
questions.expected: the wavy folded layer stiffens it
questions.memo: The corrugated (folded, wavy) middle layer stiffens cardboard while staying light.

questions.question: Rolling a flat sheet into a round shape to stiffen it is called ____.
questions.memo: Tubing means rolling a sheet into a tube to stiffen it.

questions.question: Why do cranes and towers have many diagonal bars?
options: The triangles make them stiff and stable
To use more steel for fun

questions.question: Gussets and webs can be added at joints to strengthen a frame.

questions.question: Which change would stiffen a thin steel ruler the most?
options: Bending an L-shape along its length
questions.expected: Bending an L-shape along its length
questions.memo: Adding a fold or bend along the length (changing the cross-section) greatly stiffens a thin strip.

questions.question: A shape that keeps its form and does not bend easily is called ____.
questions.memo: Rigid means stiff — it keeps its shape under load.

questions.question: Sort each method by what it mainly does to stiffen a structure.

items.text: Adding a diagonal brace to a square

questions.expected: Pleating and corrugating are folding; rolling into a dowel is tubing; adding a diagonal is triangulation.

questions.question: The main reason to stiffen a structure is to…

questions.question: Triangulation is used in roof trusses, pylons and cranes.
questions.memo: Triangulation gives rigidity to trusses, pylons and cranes.

questions.question: Which everyday item is stiffened by corrugation (folding)?

questions.question: Triangles are used because, unlike squares, they do not ____ out of shape.

questions.question: Gussets are added to a frame mainly to…
questions.memo: Gussets reinforce the joints where members meet, strengthening the frame.

TECH.G7.ST.A4.title: Frame structures & stability
TECH.G7.ST.A4.description: Structures (CAPS G7 T2) — Structures: Frame structures & stability.

questions.question: What makes a structure 'stable'?
options: It does not easily topple over
questions.expected: It does not easily topple over
questions.memo: Stability means a structure resists toppling over.

questions.question: A wide base makes a structure…
questions.memo: A wider base spreads the support and makes a structure more stable.

questions.question: A low centre of gravity makes a structure…
questions.memo: Keeping the weight low (low centre of gravity) makes a structure more stable.

questions.question: A tall, narrow, top-heavy structure topples more easily.

questions.question: Why are cell phone towers often triangulated?
options: To give them strength, rigidity and stability
questions.expected: To give them strength, rigidity and stability
questions.memo: Triangulation gives towers the strength, rigidity and stability they need to stand up to wind.

questions.question: The point where all the weight of a structure seems to act is its centre of ____.
questions.memo: The centre of gravity is where the weight seems concentrated; keeping it low aids stability.

questions.question: To make a tall model tower more stable, you should…
questions.memo: Widening the base lowers the chance of toppling — improving stability.

questions.question: Adding heavy weights to the top of a structure improves its stability.
questions.memo: Weight at the top raises the centre of gravity and makes a structure LESS stable.

questions.question: Wind is a force that acts on a tall tower. To resist it, designers use…
options: triangulation and a wide, anchored base
questions.expected: triangulation and a wide, anchored base
questions.memo: Triangulation plus a wide, anchored base helps a tower resist wind without toppling.

questions.question: A structure with a wide base and low weight is more ____.
questions.memo: Wide base + low centre of gravity = greater stability.

questions.question: Which structure is the most stable?
options: A tall thin pole on a small foot
questions.memo: A pyramid has a wide base and low centre of gravity, making it very stable.

questions.question: Triangulation adds rigidity, which also helps a frame structure stay stable.
questions.memo: Rigidity from triangulation keeps the frame from racking, helping overall stability.

questions.question: A racing car is built low and wide mainly to…
options: keep a low centre of gravity for stability
questions.expected: keep a low centre of gravity for stability
questions.memo: Low and wide gives a low centre of gravity and broad base — stable at speed.

questions.question: Disguising a cell phone tower as a tree mainly reduces…
questions.memo: Disguising towers reduces visual pollution so they blend into the environment.

questions.question: Sort each change by its effect on a tower's stability.

items.text: Add a heavy load on top

questions.expected: Widening the base and lowering the weight add stability; top weight and tall-narrow shapes reduce it.
questions.memo: Stability rises with a wider base and a lower centre of gravity; it falls when top-heavy or tall and narrow.

questions.question: Internal cross-bracing in a frame mainly improves…
questions.memo: Cross-bracing triangulates the frame, improving rigidity and stability.

questions.question: A structure can be strong but still topple if it is unstable.
questions.memo: Strength stops it breaking; stability stops it toppling — they are different needs.

questions.question: Mine headgear and windmills are strengthened by…
questions.memo: Tall frame structures like headgear and windmills use triangulation for strength and stability.

questions.question: A structure that easily falls over has poor ____.
questions.memo: Easily toppling means poor stability.

questions.question: Why is a tightrope walker's long pole helpful for balance?
options: It lowers and spreads the centre of gravity to aid stability
questions.expected: It lowers and spreads the centre of gravity to aid stability
questions.memo: A long pole spreads weight and helps keep the centre of gravity over the rope, aiding stability.

TECH.G7.MS.A1.title: Levers & mechanical advantage
TECH.G7.MS.A1.description: Mechanical Systems & Control (CAPS G7 T1) — Mechanical systems & control: Levers & mechanical advantage.
TECH.G7.MS.A1.recovery_strategy: A lever's class depends on where the fulcrum, load and effort are placed.

questions.question: What is a lever?
options: A stiff bar that turns about a pivot to move a load
questions.expected: A stiff bar that turns about a pivot to move a load
questions.memo: A lever is a rigid bar that pivots about a fulcrum to move a load with an effort.

questions.question: The fixed point a lever turns about is called the…
questions.memo: The fulcrum (pivot) is the fixed point about which a lever turns.

questions.question: In a FIRST-class lever, the fulcrum is…
options: between the effort and the load
questions.expected: between the effort and the load
questions.memo: First-class lever: the fulcrum sits between the effort and the load (like a seesaw).

questions.question: In a SECOND-class lever, the load is…
options: between the fulcrum and the effort
questions.expected: between the fulcrum and the effort
questions.memo: Second-class lever: the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort (like a wheelbarrow).

questions.question: In a THIRD-class lever, the effort is…
options: between the fulcrum and the load
questions.expected: between the fulcrum and the load
questions.memo: Third-class lever: the effort is between the fulcrum and the load (like tweezers).

questions.question: What is 'mechanical advantage'?
options: When a machine lets a small effort move a big load
questions.expected: When a machine lets a small effort move a big load
questions.memo: Mechanical advantage means a small effort can move a larger load.

questions.question: A second-class lever always gives a mechanical advantage.
questions.memo: Because the load is closer to the fulcrum than the effort, a second-class lever always has MA greater than 1.

questions.question: A third-class lever never gives a mechanical advantage greater than 1.
questions.memo: In a third-class lever the effort is closer to the fulcrum, so MA is always less than 1.

questions.question: A wheelbarrow is an example of which lever?
questions.memo: A wheelbarrow has the load between the wheel (fulcrum) and the handles (effort) — second class.

questions.question: A seesaw is an example of which lever?
questions.memo: A seesaw has the pivot in the middle, between the two people — first class.

questions.question: A pair of tweezers is which class of lever?
questions.memo: Tweezers have the effort between the fulcrum and the load — third class.

questions.question: The thing a lever moves is called the ____.
questions.memo: The load is the resistance or weight the lever moves; the effort is the force you apply.

questions.question: The force you apply to a lever is called the ____.
questions.memo: Effort is the force applied; load is what it moves; fulcrum is the pivot.

questions.question: Moving the effort further from the fulcrum on a first-class lever…
questions.memo: A longer effort arm increases mechanical advantage on a first-class lever.

questions.question: In a first-class lever, the mechanical advantage depends on where the fulcrum is.
questions.memo: Moving the fulcrum changes the effort and load arm lengths, changing the mechanical advantage.

questions.question: Order the three parts of a lever from the names used in Technology.
questions.memo: A lever has three parts: the effort you apply, the fulcrum it pivots on, and the load it moves.

questions.question: Sort each tool by its lever class.
questions.expected: Seesaw and crowbar are first class; wheelbarrow is second class; tweezers are third class.
questions.memo: First: fulcrum in the middle. Second: load in the middle. Third: effort in the middle.

questions.question: Which lever class is used to get a strong gripping force in a nutcracker?
questions.memo: A nutcracker is a second-class lever (load between fulcrum and effort), giving a strong force.

questions.question: Why use a long crowbar to lift a heavy rock?
options: The long effort arm gives a bigger mechanical advantage
questions.expected: The long effort arm gives a bigger mechanical advantage
questions.memo: A long effort arm increases mechanical advantage so a small effort lifts a big load.

questions.question: A machine that lets a small effort move a large load gives a mechanical ____.
questions.memo: Mechanical advantage = a small effort moves a larger load.

TECH.G7.MS.A2.title: Linkages in tools
TECH.G7.MS.A2.description: Mechanical Systems & Control (CAPS G7 T1) — Mechanical systems & control: Linkages in tools.
TECH.G7.MS.A2.recovery_strategy: Linked levers join two levers so they work together, like the blades of scissors.

questions.question: What is a linkage?
options: Levers joined together to work as a system
questions.expected: Levers joined together to work as a system
questions.memo: A linkage is two or more levers joined so they move together.

questions.question: A pair of scissors is made of…
questions.memo: Scissors are two first-class levers linked at a central pivot.

questions.question: A pair of pliers works as…
questions.memo: Pliers are linked first-class levers — squeezing the handles grips with the jaws.

questions.question: An office hole punch is an example of linked…
questions.memo: A hole punch uses linked second-class levers to give a strong punching force.

questions.question: A light-duty office stapler is an example of a linked…
questions.memo: A light stapler is a third-class lever — the effort is between the pivot and the staple.

questions.question: Linkages can change the direction or size of a movement.
questions.memo: Linkages transfer and can change the direction or amount of movement between parts.

questions.question: Two or more levers joined to move together form a ____.
questions.memo: A linkage is levers joined to move together.

questions.question: Hedge-trimming shears with long handles and short blades give…
questions.memo: Long handles and short blades give linked levers a large cutting force.

questions.question: Why do nutcrackers and bolt cutters have long handles?
options: To increase the force at the jaws
questions.expected: To increase the force at the jaws
questions.memo: Long handles give a bigger mechanical advantage, increasing the gripping/cutting force.

questions.question: A more complex linkage can have more than one pivot.
questions.memo: Complex linkages use several pivots to make more complicated movements.

questions.question: In scissors, where is the pivot (fulcrum)?
options: In the middle, between handles and blades
questions.expected: In the middle, between handles and blades
questions.memo: The pivot of scissors is central — making each side a first-class lever.

questions.question: Pliers and scissors are both linked ____-class levers.
questions.memo: Both pliers and scissors are pairs of first-class levers.

questions.question: Which everyday tool is a linkage of two levers?
questions.memo: Pliers are a linkage of two levers; a bulb, magnet and battery are not levers.

questions.question: Tweezers are a single third-class lever rather than a linked pair.
questions.memo: Tweezers are two third-class levers linked together (joined at one end).

questions.question: Sort each tool by the lever class of its linkage.
questions.expected: Scissors and pliers are linked first-class; a hole punch is linked second-class; a light stapler is linked third-class.
questions.memo: Scissors/pliers = first class; hole punch = second class; light stapler/tweezers = third class.

questions.question: The main purpose of a linkage in a tool is to…
options: pass on or change a movement or force
questions.expected: pass on or change a movement or force
questions.memo: Linkages transfer and change movement or force between the parts of a tool.

questions.question: Squeezing the handles of pliers makes the jaws move closer together.
questions.memo: The linked levers turn handle movement into jaw movement to grip.

questions.question: Bigger handles on bolt cutters mainly change the…
questions.memo: Longer handles increase the force the linkage delivers at the jaws.

questions.question: A tool with several pivots is a ____ linkage.
questions.memo: More than one pivot makes a complex linkage.

questions.question: Garden secateurs (pruning shears) are linked levers designed mainly to…
options: cut branches with a strong force
questions.expected: cut branches with a strong force
questions.memo: Secateurs are linked levers that give a strong cutting force at the blades.

TECH.G7.MS.A3.title: Pneumatics & hydraulics
TECH.G7.MS.A3.description: Mechanical Systems & Control (CAPS G7 T1) — Mechanical systems & control: Pneumatics & hydraulics.
TECH.G7.MS.A3.recovery_strategy: Pneumatics use air; hydraulics use liquid; both push force along a tube.

questions.question: What does a PNEUMATIC system use to transfer force?
questions.memo: Pneumatic systems use compressed air (a gas) to transfer force.

questions.question: What does a HYDRAULIC system use to transfer force?
options: A liquid such as water or oil
questions.expected: A liquid such as water or oil
questions.memo: Hydraulic systems use a liquid (water or oil) to transfer force.

questions.question: In these systems, force is transferred through a tube from one syringe to another.
questions.memo: Pushing one syringe pushes the fluid through the tube, moving the other syringe.

questions.question: Which fluid can be squashed (compressed) more easily?
questions.memo: Gases like air are compressible; liquids like water are almost incompressible.

questions.question: Liquids are almost impossible to squash, which makes hydraulics feel firm.
questions.memo: Liquids are incompressible, so hydraulic systems feel solid and transfer force well.

questions.question: Pushing a small syringe connected to a LARGER syringe will…
options: move the large piston with more force but less distance
questions.expected: move the large piston with more force but less distance
questions.memo: A small input to a large cylinder gives more force over a shorter movement — a mechanical advantage.

questions.question: A system that uses compressed air to do work is called ____.
questions.memo: Pneumatic = powered by compressed air.

questions.question: A system that uses a liquid to do work is called ____.
questions.memo: Hydraulic = powered by a liquid.

questions.question: Which machine uses hydraulics?
questions.memo: Excavator arms use hydraulic cylinders to push and lift with great force.

questions.question: Why might 'Jaws of Life' rescue tools use hydraulics?
options: To produce a very large force to cut or spread metal
questions.expected: To produce a very large force to cut or spread metal
questions.memo: Hydraulics multiply force, giving rescue tools the power to cut and spread metal.

questions.question: Air brakes on a bus are an example of a pneumatic system.
questions.memo: Air (pneumatic) brakes use compressed air to operate the brakes.

questions.question: A pneumatic system feels 'springy' compared with a hydraulic one because…
questions.memo: Air compresses, so pneumatic systems feel springy; hydraulics feel firm.

questions.question: Force is transferred between two syringes through the connecting ____.
questions.memo: The fluid carries the force through the connecting tube.

questions.question: Two EQUAL-sized syringes connected by a tube will move…
options: the same distance as each other
questions.expected: the same distance as each other
questions.memo: Equal syringes move equal distances; force and movement are unchanged.

questions.question: Sort each example into 'Pneumatic' or 'Hydraulic'.
questions.expected: Air brakes and a pump are pneumatic; an excavator arm and a car jack are hydraulic.
questions.memo: Pneumatic systems use air; hydraulic systems use a liquid.

questions.question: Both pneumatic and hydraulic systems are used to…
questions.memo: Both transfer force through a fluid to do useful work, often with a mechanical advantage.

questions.question: Hydraulic systems can produce very large forces, which is why they lift heavy loads.
questions.memo: Because liquids are incompressible and force can be multiplied, hydraulics lift heavy loads.

questions.question: Which is an advantage of hydraulics over pneumatics for heavy lifting?
options: The liquid does not compress, so movement is firm and controlled
questions.expected: The liquid does not compress, so movement is firm and controlled
questions.memo: Incompressible liquid gives firm, controlled, powerful movement for heavy lifting.

questions.question: Gases can be compressed, but liquids are nearly ____.
questions.memo: Liquids are nearly incompressible; gases compress easily.

questions.question: A dentist's chair that is raised by foot-pumping a lever most likely uses a…
questions.memo: Dentist and barber chairs are commonly raised by a hydraulic system pumped with the foot.

TECH.G7.MS.A4.title: Cranks & pulleys
TECH.G7.MS.A4.description: Mechanical Systems & Control (CAPS G7 T1) — Mechanical systems & control: Cranks & pulleys.
TECH.G7.MS.A4.recovery_strategy: A crank turns round motion into back-and-forth; a pulley is a wheel turning on an axle.

questions.question: What does a crank do?
options: Changes round (rotary) motion into back-and-forth (reciprocating) motion
questions.expected: Changes round (rotary) motion into back-and-forth (reciprocating) motion
questions.memo: A crank converts rotary motion into reciprocating (back-and-forth) motion, and vice versa.

questions.question: A pulley is a type of…

questions.question: A crank is an adaptation of a second-class lever.

questions.question: What is one common use of a pulley?

questions.memo: Pulleys are used to lift loads and to change the direction of a pulling force.

questions.question: A single fixed pulley mainly changes the…

questions.question: A crank turns rotary motion into ____ motion.

questions.question: A pulley can be used to make lifting a load easier.
questions.memo: Pulley systems can give a mechanical advantage, making lifting easier.

questions.question: Where would you find a crank in everyday life?

questions.question: A flagpole uses a pulley at the top to…
options: raise and lower the flag by pulling a rope
questions.expected: raise and lower the flag by pulling a rope
questions.memo: A flagpole pulley lets you raise the flag by pulling down on the rope.

questions.question: All complex machines are built from combinations of simple mechanisms.
questions.memo: Complex machinery is made by combining simple mechanisms like levers, cranks and pulleys.

questions.question: A wheel turning on an axle with a rope around it is a ____.
questions.memo: That description is a pulley — a wheel-and-axle with a rope or belt.

questions.question: A hand drill turned by a handle uses a crank to…
options: turn the handle's motion into rotation of the drill
questions.expected: turn the handle's motion into rotation of the drill
questions.memo: The crank handle converts your hand movement into rotation of the drill bit.

questions.question: Why might a crane combine a frame structure with a pulley and crank?
options: The frame supports it while the pulley and crank lift and move loads
questions.expected: The frame supports it while the pulley and crank lift and move loads
questions.memo: A crane uses a rigid triangulated frame plus a pulley and crank mechanism to lift loads.

questions.question: A pulley can change both the direction and (with more wheels) the amount of force.
questions.memo: A fixed pulley changes direction; adding moveable pulleys multiplies the force.

questions.question: Sort each mechanism by what it mainly does.

items.text: Turns rotary motion into back-and-forth motion
Lifts a load with a rope over a wheel

questions.expected: A crank changes rotary to reciprocating motion (bicycle pedal); a pulley lifts loads with a rope (flagpole).
questions.memo: Crank = converts rotary↔reciprocating motion; pulley = wheel-and-axle for lifting and changing force direction.

questions.question: Levers, cranks and pulleys are all examples of…
questions.memo: Levers, cranks and pulleys are simple mechanisms that make work easier.

questions.question: A pulley belt can transfer rotation from one wheel to another.
questions.memo: A belt around two pulleys transfers rotation from a driver wheel to a driven wheel.

questions.question: To lift a load straight up by pulling down on a rope, you would use a…
questions.memo: A fixed pulley changes your downward pull into an upward lift.

questions.question: A crank is described as an adapted ____-class lever.
questions.memo: CAPS treats the crank as an adapted second-class lever.

questions.question: Two pulleys joined by a belt are used to…
options: transfer rotation from one shaft to another
questions.expected: transfer rotation from one shaft to another
questions.memo: A belt over two pulleys carries rotation from a driver wheel to a driven wheel.

TECH.G7.ES.A1.title: Magnetism & magnetic materials
TECH.G7.ES.A1.description: Electrical Systems & Control (CAPS G7 T3) — Electrical systems & control: Magnetism & magnetic materials.

questions.question: What is a magnet?

An object that gives off light

questions.question: Steel is an iron alloy and is attracted by a magnet.

questions.question: Two common shapes of permanent magnet are…

questions.question: Metals like iron, steel and ____ are attracted by a magnet.

questions.question: Iron filings sprinkled near a magnet line up to show…

questions.question: A magnet can attract some metals but not non-metals.

questions.question: Why must you avoid a copper-coated steel paper clip when testing magnets?
options: The steel inside still sticks, giving a wrong result

questions.question: A scrap dealer can use a magnet to separate…

questions.expected: iron and steel from copper and aluminium
questions.memo: A magnet picks up magnetic metals (iron/steel), separating them from non-magnetic ones.

questions.question: Wood and paper are attracted by a strong magnet.

questions.question: Which set lists ONLY magnetic materials?

questions.question: Sort each material into 'Attracted by a magnet' or 'Not attracted'.
questions.expected: Iron and steel are attracted; copper, aluminium and plastic are not.
questions.memo: Magnetic: iron, steel, nickel. Not magnetic: copper, aluminium, lead, brass, and all non-metals.

questions.question: A horseshoe magnet is shaped like a U mainly to…

questions.expected: bring both poles close together for a stronger pull

questions.question: Some metals stick to magnets and some do not.

questions.question: To test which metals are magnetic, you would…

questions.question: Bar and ____ are two common shapes of permanent magnet.

questions.question: Recycling scrap metal is valuable to society, but is harmed by…

questions.expected: thieves who steal copper wire and manhole covers

TECH.G7.ES.A2.title: Simple electric circuits & symbols

questions.expected: A complete loop with a power source

questions.question: What does a switch do in a circuit?

questions.question: Which is an OUTPUT device in a simple circuit?

questions.question: What is a conductor?

questions.question: A device drawn as a circle with a cross is the symbol for a ____.
questions.memo: The lamp/bulb symbol is a circle with a cross inside.

questions.question: Why do we use symbols when drawing a circuit?
options: So everyone can read the circuit the same simple way
questions.expected: So everyone can read the circuit the same simple way
questions.memo: Standard symbols let anyone read a circuit diagram quickly and clearly.

questions.question: Copper wire is used in circuits because it is a good…
questions.memo: Copper conducts electricity well, so it is used for wires.

questions.question: Plastic around a wire is an insulator that keeps the current inside.

questions.question: In the GET band, circuits must be battery powered with a maximum of…
