questions.question: A material that does NOT let electricity flow is an ____.
questions.memo: Insulators (plastic, rubber) block current; conductors (metals) allow it.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of parts in a simple lighting circuit?
options: Cell → switch → bulb → back to cell
questions.expected: Cell → switch → bulb → back to cell
questions.memo: Current flows from the cell, through the switch and bulb, and back to the cell — a complete loop.

questions.question: A buzzer is an output device that turns electricity into sound.
questions.memo: A buzzer is an output that converts electrical energy into sound.

questions.question: Sort each component by its job in a circuit.
questions.expected: The cell is the source; the switch is the control; the bulb and buzzer are outputs.
questions.memo: Source = cell; control = switch; output = bulb, buzzer or motor.

questions.question: Put the steps to make a bulb light up in order.

items.text: Connect a wire from the cell to the switch
Connect the switch to the bulb
Connect the bulb back to the cell
Close the switch so current flows

questions.memo: Build a complete loop (cell → switch → bulb → cell), then close the switch to let current flow.

questions.question: Which would NOT conduct electricity?
questions.memo: Rubber is an insulator; copper, steel and aluminium are conductors.

questions.question: A circuit diagram uses agreed symbols instead of pictures of the real parts.
questions.memo: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols, which are quicker and clearer than drawings of the parts.

questions.question: If a bulb does not light, a likely cause is…
options: a break in the circuit or the switch is off
the wire is too short by 1mm
the cell is the wrong colour
questions.expected: a break in the circuit or the switch is off
questions.memo: A bulb won't light if the loop is broken or the switch is open (off).

questions.question: A complete, unbroken path for current is called a ____.
questions.memo: A circuit is the complete loop the current flows around.

TECH.G7.ES.A3.title: Electromagnets
TECH.G7.ES.A3.description: Electrical Systems & Control (CAPS G7 T3) — Electrical systems & control: Electromagnets.
TECH.G7.ES.A3.recovery_strategy: An electromagnet is wire coiled around an iron core; it is magnetic only while current flows.

questions.question: How do you make a simple electromagnet?
options: Coil insulated wire around an iron core and pass current through it
questions.expected: Coil insulated wire around an iron core and pass current through it
questions.memo: An electromagnet is made by coiling insulated wire (a solenoid) around an iron core and switching on current.

questions.question: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows through the coil.
questions.memo: Switch the current off and the magnetism fades — that is the key feature of an electromagnet.

questions.question: What is a big ADVANTAGE of an electromagnet over a permanent magnet?
options: You can switch it on and off
questions.expected: You can switch it on and off
questions.memo: An electromagnet can be turned on and off, unlike a permanent magnet.

questions.question: A coil of wire used to make an electromagnet is called a…
questions.memo: A solenoid is a coil of wire; current through it creates a magnetic field.

questions.question: Why is a 'soft' iron core used instead of a hard steel bolt?
options: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily
questions.expected: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily
questions.memo: Soft iron loses its magnetism quickly when the current stops, which is what you want.

questions.question: Using a longer coil of wire makes an electromagnet stronger.
questions.memo: More turns of wire (a longer coil) make the electromagnet stronger.

questions.question: An electromagnet's magnetism disappears when you switch the current ____.
questions.memo: Switch off the current and the magnetic field fades away.

questions.question: Adding more cells (more voltage) to an electromagnet usually…
questions.memo: More current (from more cells) increases the electromagnet's strength somewhat.

questions.question: A scrap-yard crane uses an electromagnet to…
options: pick up and then drop steel by switching it on and off
questions.expected: pick up and then drop steel by switching it on and off
questions.memo: An electromagnet lets the crane grab steel and release it by switching the current off.

questions.question: Electromagnets are used in many modern technologies like motors and bells.
questions.memo: Electromagnetism is behind motors, bells, speakers and many devices.

questions.question: Wire is coiled around an iron ____ to make an electromagnet.
questions.memo: The iron core, wrapped in a coil, concentrates the magnetic field.

questions.question: Which change would NOT make an electromagnet stronger?
questions.memo: Switching off the current removes the magnetism entirely — it cannot make it stronger.

questions.question: The insulation (plastic) on the coil wire stops the coils short-circuiting each other.
questions.memo: Insulated wire keeps the current flowing around the coil instead of jumping between turns.

questions.question: Order the steps to build and use a simple electromagnet.

items.text: Wind insulated copper wire around an iron core
Connect the wire ends to a cell and a switch
Close the switch so current flows and it becomes magnetic
Open the switch to release the load

questions.memo: Coil the wire on the core, connect to a cell and switch, close to magnetise, open to release.

questions.question: Sort each statement: does it describe an electromagnet or a permanent magnet?

items.text: Can be switched on and off
Needs an electric current to work

questions.expected: Electromagnets switch on/off and need current; permanent magnets are always magnetic.
questions.memo: Electromagnet = magnetic only with current, switchable. Permanent magnet = always magnetic.

questions.question: Adding a light bulb to the electromagnet circuit can…
options: show when the magnet is switched on
questions.expected: show when the magnet is switched on
questions.memo: A bulb in the circuit acts as an indicator that the electromagnet is on.

questions.question: A nail can be used as the iron core of a simple electromagnet.
questions.memo: A 'relatively soft' iron nail works as a simple core (softer than a hard steel bolt).

questions.question: The main parts of an electromagnet are…
options: a coil of wire, an iron core and a power source
questions.expected: a coil of wire, an iron core and a power source
questions.memo: An electromagnet needs a coil (solenoid), an iron core, and a current source.

questions.question: More turns of wire and more cells make an electromagnet ____.
questions.memo: Both more coils and more current strengthen an electromagnet.

questions.question: Why is the ability to switch off useful for a scrap-sorting magnet?
options: It can release the metals it has picked up
questions.expected: It can release the metals it has picked up
questions.memo: Switching off lets the electromagnet drop the sorted metal — a permanent magnet could not.

TECH.G7.PR.A1.title: Processing food
TECH.G7.PR.A1.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G7 T4) — Processing, society & environment: Processing food.
TECH.G7.PR.A1.recovery_strategy: Processing changes raw ingredients into a useful product, like turning flour into bread.

questions.question: What does 'processing' mean in Technology?
options: Changing raw materials into a more useful product
questions.expected: Changing raw materials into a more useful product
questions.memo: Processing changes raw materials into a more useful form — like turning flour into bread.

questions.question: Processing food means…
options: preparing or changing food so it is useful to eat
questions.expected: preparing or changing food so it is useful to eat
questions.memo: Food processing prepares or changes ingredients into edible, useful products.

questions.question: A nutritious meal gives the body the food it needs to stay healthy.
questions.memo: Nutritious food supplies the nutrients the body needs for health.

questions.question: When designing emergency food for a refugee camp, an important factor is that the food is…
options: nutritious and easy to prepare in basic conditions
questions.expected: nutritious and easy to prepare in basic conditions
questions.memo: Emergency food must be nutritious and preparable under the basic conditions of a camp.

questions.question: Changing raw ingredients into a meal is an example of food ____.
questions.memo: Turning ingredients into a meal is processing.

questions.question: Why write down the 'sequence of manufacture' for preparing food?
options: So the steps are done in the right order
questions.expected: So the steps are done in the right order
questions.memo: A sequence of manufacture lists the steps in the correct order so the product is made properly.

questions.question: When evaluating a prepared food item, you might judge its…
questions.memo: Food is evaluated on flavour, texture and nutritional value.

questions.question: A design brief for emergency food should state the types and quantities of food needed.
questions.memo: The brief sets out what food is needed and how much, for the number of people.

questions.question: Feeding 100 refugees needs you to think about…
questions.memo: Designing food for 100 people means working out the quantities of ingredients.

questions.question: The order in which steps are done to make a product is the sequence of ____.
questions.memo: The sequence of manufacture is the ordered list of making steps.

questions.question: Put the steps of preparing a simple food item in a sensible order.
questions.memo: Gather ingredients, measure them, prepare the item, then evaluate it — a sensible sequence of manufacture.

questions.question: Processing can make raw materials safer, tastier or last longer.
questions.memo: Processing often improves safety, taste or shelf life of raw materials.

questions.question: Which is an example of processing a raw material into food?
options: Grinding wheat into flour and baking bread
Looking at a field of wheat
questions.expected: Grinding wheat into flour and baking bread
questions.memo: Grinding and baking change the raw wheat into a useful product — processing.

questions.question: A balanced emergency meal should mainly provide…
options: energy and nutrients to keep people healthy
questions.expected: energy and nutrients to keep people healthy
questions.memo: Emergency meals must supply energy and nutrients for health.

questions.question: Sort each activity: is it 'Processing food' or not?

items.text: Drying fruit to make it last
Drawing a picture of a loaf

questions.expected: Cooking maize and drying fruit change the food (processing); looking and drawing do not.
questions.memo: Processing changes the raw material; simply observing or drawing it does not.

questions.question: Refugees in an emergency mainly need shelter, food and clean water.
questions.memo: Basic emergency needs are shelter, food and water.

questions.question: Why must emergency food be easy to prepare?
options: Camp conditions are basic, with limited equipment
questions.expected: Camp conditions are basic, with limited equipment
questions.memo: In a camp, cooking facilities are basic, so the food must be simple to prepare.

questions.question: Food is evaluated on flavour, texture and ____ value.
questions.memo: Nutritional value is a key way to evaluate food.

questions.question: Designing food for many people is part of the design process because you must…
options: investigate needs, write a brief, make and evaluate
questions.expected: investigate needs, write a brief, make and evaluate
questions.memo: Even food design follows the design process: investigate, brief, make, evaluate.

questions.question: A 'design brief' for food sets out what is needed before you start cooking.
questions.memo: The design brief states the requirements (types and quantities of food) before making begins.

TECH.G7.PR.A2.title: Materials & textiles
TECH.G7.PR.A2.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G7 T4) — Processing, society & environment: Materials & textiles.
TECH.G7.PR.A2.recovery_strategy: Different materials and textiles suit different jobs because of their properties.

questions.question: A textile is best described as…
questions.memo: A textile is a cloth or fabric, like canvas, cotton or wool.

questions.question: Which property would matter most for a tent fabric in the rain?
questions.memo: A tent fabric must be waterproof to keep the rain out.

questions.question: Different materials are chosen for different jobs based on their properties.
questions.memo: We pick materials by their properties (strength, waterproofing, flexibility) to suit the job.

questions.question: Why investigate the 'burning characteristics' of a textile for firefighters?
options: So the clothing resists catching fire
questions.expected: So the clothing resists catching fire
questions.memo: Firefighters need fabrics that resist burning, so burning behaviour is investigated.

questions.question: Canvas can be made waterproof by…
options: treating it with a waterproofing chemical
questions.expected: treating it with a waterproofing chemical
questions.memo: Applying a waterproofing chemical stops water passing through canvas.

questions.question: Cloth or fabric used to make clothing and shelters is called a ____.
questions.memo: Textiles are fabrics used for clothing, tents and more.

questions.question: Specialised workers like firefighters wear clothing made of textiles that are…
questions.memo: Firefighters' clothing must resist heat and flames.

questions.question: A material's properties decide whether it is suitable for a particular use.
questions.memo: Suitability for a use depends on the material's properties.

questions.question: Which property helps a raincoat keep you dry?
questions.memo: A waterproof material keeps water out — essential for a raincoat.

questions.question: For NSRI sea-rescue clothing, an important property is that it is…
options: water-resistant and keeps the wearer warm
questions.expected: water-resistant and keeps the wearer warm
questions.memo: Sea-rescue clothing must resist water and keep the wearer warm.

questions.question: A material that does not let water through is ____.
questions.memo: Waterproof = water cannot pass through.

questions.question: All textiles burn at the same speed.
questions.memo: Different textiles have different burning characteristics — some resist fire far better.

questions.question: To choose a fabric for an emergency shelter, you would test it for…
questions.memo: Shelter fabric must be strong and waterproof to protect people.

questions.question: Sort each property by whether it suits a rain shelter fabric.
questions.expected: Waterproof and strong are good; full of holes or dissolving in water are not.
questions.memo: Match the material's properties to the job: a shelter fabric must be waterproof and strong.

questions.question: Which material property means it can bend without breaking?
questions.memo: Flexibility is the ability to bend without breaking.

questions.question: Choosing the wrong material can make a product fail at its job.
questions.memo: A material whose properties don't suit the job can cause the product to fail.

questions.question: A good shelter material should be…
options: sturdy, waterproof and easy to transport
questions.expected: sturdy, waterproof and easy to transport
questions.memo: Shelter material should be sturdy, waterproof and easy to move and erect.

questions.question: Firefighters need clothing made from ____-resistant textiles.
questions.memo: Flame-resistant textiles protect firefighters from burning.

questions.question: Why test materials before using them in a design?
options: To check they have the right properties for the job
questions.expected: To check they have the right properties for the job
questions.memo: Testing confirms a material's properties suit the design before you commit to it.

questions.question: Canvas is a textile that can be treated to become waterproof.
questions.memo: Canvas can be chemically treated to make it waterproof for tents and covers.

TECH.G7.PR.A3.title: Indigenous technology
TECH.G7.PR.A3.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G7 T4) — Processing, society & environment: Indigenous technology.
TECH.G7.PR.A3.recovery_strategy: Indigenous builders use local materials that are appropriate and kind to the environment.

questions.question: What is 'indigenous technology'?
options: Knowledge and methods developed by local people over time
questions.expected: Knowledge and methods developed by local people over time
questions.memo: Indigenous technology is the knowledge and methods local/traditional communities developed over generations.

questions.question: Indigenous builders often use local materials that are readily available.
questions.memo: Indigenous building uses materials that are local, available and appropriate.

questions.question: A common feature of indigenous building materials is that they are…
options: environmentally friendly and appropriate to the area
questions.expected: environmentally friendly and appropriate to the area
questions.memo: Indigenous materials tend to be environmentally friendly and suited to the local climate.

questions.question: Why is indigenous knowledge valuable to study?
options: It shows clever, sustainable ways to meet needs
questions.expected: It shows clever, sustainable ways to meet needs
questions.memo: Indigenous knowledge offers clever, sustainable, low-impact ways to meet needs.

questions.question: Indigenous building often uses ____ materials found nearby.
questions.memo: Indigenous builders use locally available materials.

questions.question: An example of an indigenous building material is…
questions.memo: Traditional houses often use mud, grass, thatch and reeds — local natural materials.

questions.question: Indigenous people have the right to protection of their traditional knowledge (intellectual property).
questions.memo: Indigenous intellectual property rights protect traditional knowledge and methods.

questions.question: Compared with informal-settlement shacks, indigenous houses are often…
options: better suited to the climate and environment
questions.expected: better suited to the climate and environment
questions.memo: Indigenous designs are often well suited to local climate using appropriate materials.

questions.question: Using materials that do not harm nature makes a design environmentally ____.
questions.memo: Environmentally friendly designs avoid harming nature.

questions.question: Why do indigenous designs often suit the local climate well?
options: They were developed over time to fit local conditions
questions.expected: They were developed over time to fit local conditions
questions.memo: Generations of refining mean indigenous designs fit local conditions and climate.

questions.question: Thatch (dried grass) roofing is an example of indigenous building technology.
questions.memo: Thatch roofing is a traditional, indigenous building method using local grass.

questions.question: Sustainable use of materials means…
options: using resources so they last for the future
using them all up at once
questions.expected: using resources so they last for the future
questions.memo: Sustainability means using resources carefully so they remain for the future.

questions.question: Sort each material into 'Indigenous/local' or 'Modern/manufactured'.
questions.expected: Thatch and mud bricks are indigenous/local; steel and factory glass are modern/manufactured.
questions.memo: Indigenous materials are local and natural (thatch, mud); modern materials are manufactured (steel, glass).

questions.question: Learning from indigenous technology can help modern designers to…
options: build in more sustainable, low-cost ways
questions.expected: build in more sustainable, low-cost ways
questions.memo: Indigenous methods inspire sustainable, affordable, low-impact modern design.

questions.question: Indigenous technology never has anything useful to teach modern engineers.
questions.memo: Indigenous technology offers valuable, sustainable lessons for modern design.

questions.question: Different coexisting 'knowledge systems' means…
options: both modern and traditional knowledge can be valued together
questions.expected: both modern and traditional knowledge can be valued together
questions.memo: We can value modern science and indigenous knowledge side by side.

questions.question: Traditional knowledge passed down by local people is ____ knowledge.
questions.memo: Indigenous knowledge is the traditional knowledge of local communities.

questions.question: Why are indigenous materials often a good environmental choice?
options: They are local, natural and biodegradable
questions.expected: They are local, natural and biodegradable
questions.memo: Local, natural materials use little transport and break down naturally.

questions.question: Indigenous houses are usually built from materials found close by.
questions.memo: Indigenous building relies on nearby, readily available materials.

questions.question: Respecting indigenous intellectual property means…
options: giving credit and rights for traditional knowledge
questions.expected: giving credit and rights for traditional knowledge
questions.memo: Indigenous IP rights mean traditional knowledge is credited and protected.

TECH.G7.PR.A4.title: Impact & bias in technology
TECH.G7.PR.A4.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G7 T4) — Processing, society & environment: Impact & bias in technology.
TECH.G7.PR.A4.recovery_strategy: Technology can help or harm people and the environment, and can favour some groups over others.

questions.question: Technology can have which kinds of impact on society?
questions.memo: Technology has both positive and negative impacts on people and the environment.

questions.question: What is 'bias' in technology?
options: When a product favours or disadvantages a group of people
questions.expected: When a product favours or disadvantages a group of people
questions.memo: Bias means a technology unfairly favours some groups or disadvantages others.

questions.question: Recycling scrap metal can be valuable to society.
questions.memo: Recycling metal saves resources and creates value — a positive impact.

questions.question: A negative impact of technology could be…
questions.memo: Pollution is a negative impact technology can have on the environment.

questions.question: A positive impact of technology could be…
questions.memo: Better communication and medicine are positive impacts of technology.

questions.question: When a design unfairly favours one group over another, it shows ____.
questions.memo: Bias is unfair favouring or disadvantaging of groups by a technology.

questions.question: Stealing copper cables is a negative, criminal impact linked to scrap metal.
questions.memo: Cable theft is a criminal, negative impact tied to the scrap-metal trade.

questions.question: A school recycling scheme can raise funds by…
questions.memo: Collecting cans, paper and plastic for recycling can raise funds and reduce waste.

questions.question: A product that only works for right-handed people shows…
questions.memo: A right-handed-only product disadvantages left-handed users — that is bias.

questions.question: Reusing and recycling materials helps the ____.
questions.memo: Recycling and reusing reduce waste and protect the environment.

questions.question: We should weigh up both the good and bad effects of a technology.
questions.memo: Good technology decisions weigh positive and negative impacts together.

questions.question: Which is the BEST way to reduce technology's impact on the environment?
questions.memo: Reduce, reuse, recycle lowers waste and environmental impact.

questions.question: Sort each effect of technology as 'Positive' or 'Negative'.

items.text: Recycling creates jobs and saves resources
Cable theft cuts off phone lines

questions.expected: Recycling and medicine are positive; pollution and theft are negative.
questions.memo: Technology brings both benefits (jobs, medicine) and harms (pollution, crime) — weigh both.

questions.question: Sorting recyclable metal into types (e.g. ferrous and non-ferrous) is useful because…
questions.memo: Sorting metals by type raises their recycling value.

questions.question: A technology that helps one group but harms another shows bias.
questions.memo: Helping some while harming others is a sign of bias in technology.

questions.question: Why think about the environment when designing a product?
options: So the product does not damage the planet
questions.expected: So the product does not damage the planet
questions.memo: Considering the environment helps avoid lasting damage to the planet.

questions.question: Cans, paper and plastic can all be collected for ____.
questions.memo: These materials are recyclable and can be collected to be reused.

questions.question: An example of weighing impacts is comparing landline and mobile phones for…
options: their advantages and disadvantages to society
questions.expected: their advantages and disadvantages to society
questions.memo: Comparing landline vs mobile means weighing each one's pros and cons for society.

questions.question: Good designers think about how their product affects different groups in society.
questions.memo: Thinking about effects on different groups helps avoid bias and harm.

questions.question: The 'three Rs' for caring for the environment are…
questions.memo: Reduce, reuse and recycle are the three Rs of environmental care.

TECH.G8.DG.A1.title: Graphics conventions
TECH.G8.DG.A1.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G8 T1) — Graphics & drawing: Graphics conventions.
TECH.G8.DG.A1.recovery_strategy: Conventions like centre lines, scaling and dimensions in mm keep drawings clear and standard.

questions.question: What is a centre line used to show on a drawing?
options: The centre of a circle, hole or symmetrical part
questions.expected: The centre of a circle, hole or symmetrical part
questions.memo: A centre line marks the centre of circles, holes and symmetrical features.

questions.question: A centre line is drawn as a…
options: chain line (long dash, dot, long dash)
questions.expected: chain line (long dash, dot, long dash)
questions.memo: Centre lines use a chain line — alternating long dashes and dots.

questions.question: In what unit are dimensions usually given on these drawings?
questions.memo: Technical drawings normally use millimetres for dimensions.

questions.question: 'Scaling down' a drawing means…
options: drawing the object smaller than real size
drawing it bigger than real size
questions.expected: drawing the object smaller than real size
questions.memo: Scaling down draws a large object smaller so it fits the page.

questions.question: 'Scaling up' a drawing means…
options: drawing a small object larger than real size
questions.expected: drawing a small object larger than real size
questions.memo: Scaling up draws a tiny object bigger so its detail can be seen.

questions.question: Conventions are agreed rules so that any reader understands a drawing the same way.
questions.memo: Conventions (line types, scale, dimensions) are shared rules for clear communication.

questions.question: Dimensions on a technical drawing are usually given in ____.
questions.memo: Millimetres (mm) are the standard unit for dimensions.

questions.question: A scale of 2:1 means the drawing is…
options: twice the size of the real object
questions.expected: twice the size of the real object
questions.memo: 2:1 means 2 units on the drawing equal 1 real unit — the drawing is double size.

questions.question: Hidden detail is shown with a dashed line, even in Grade 8.
questions.memo: Dashed lines for hidden detail is a convention that continues across the grades.

questions.question: A long-dash-dot line that marks the middle of a part is a ____ line.

questions.question: Why dimension a drawing in mm rather than guessing sizes?
options: So the part is made to the exact size
questions.expected: So the part is made to the exact size
questions.memo: Exact dimensions let the maker build the part to the correct size.

questions.question: A drawing of a tiny watch gear is best drawn using…
questions.memo: A very small object is scaled up so its detail is visible.

questions.question: Outlines are still drawn as thick, dark lines in Grade 8.
questions.memo: Thick dark outlines for visible edges remain a convention.

questions.question: Drawing a big bridge small enough to fit on paper uses scaling ____.
questions.memo: Large objects are scaled down to fit the page.

questions.question: Which is NOT a normal drawing convention?
options: Writing dimensions in random units each time
questions.expected: Writing dimensions in random units each time
questions.memo: Conventions require a consistent unit (mm); random units break the convention.

questions.question: A scale of 1:1 means…
options: the drawing is the same size as the object
questions.expected: the drawing is the same size as the object
questions.memo: 1:1 is full size — the drawing matches the real object exactly.

TECH.G8.DG.A2.title: Isometric & two-point perspective
TECH.G8.DG.A2.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G8 T1) — Graphics & drawing: Isometric & two-point perspective.
TECH.G8.DG.A2.recovery_strategy: Isometric uses a slanted grid; two-point perspective uses two vanishing points for realism.

questions.question: Isometric drawing shows three sides of an object using lines that go up at…
questions.memo: Isometric drawing uses 30° lines for the two receding directions.

questions.question: In isometric drawing, vertical edges are drawn…
questions.memo: Isometric keeps verticals vertical, with the other two directions at 30°.

questions.question: How many vanishing points does a two-point perspective drawing use?
questions.memo: Two-point perspective uses two vanishing points, one on each side.

questions.question: Two-point perspective makes a drawing look realistic, with sides shrinking towards two points.
questions.memo: Two-point perspective gives realism, with edges converging to two vanishing points.

questions.question: Isometric drawing is often done on…
questions.memo: An isometric grid of 30° lines helps draw isometric views accurately.

questions.question: Isometric drawings use lines at ____ degrees for the receding sides.
questions.memo: Isometric uses 30° for the two receding directions.

questions.question: Which technique keeps the SAME scale along all three isometric axes?
questions.memo: Isometric keeps equal scale on all three axes, unlike perspective which shrinks with distance.

questions.question: In perspective drawing, things look smaller as they get further away.
questions.memo: Perspective shrinks objects with distance, towards the vanishing point(s).

questions.question: Adding colour, texture and shading to a drawing mainly…
questions.memo: Shading, colour and texture add realism to a 3D drawing.

questions.question: A realistic 3D drawing using two vanishing points is ____-point perspective.
questions.memo: Two vanishing points = two-point perspective.

questions.question: Why might a designer use isometric rather than perspective for a working idea?
options: Isometric keeps true measurements along the axes
questions.expected: Isometric keeps true measurements along the axes
questions.memo: Isometric keeps measurable, equal scales, which helps with sizing.

questions.question: Shadows can be added to a perspective drawing to make it more realistic.
questions.memo: Shadows enhance realism in perspective drawings.

questions.question: Both isometric and perspective are ways of drawing in…
questions.memo: Isometric and perspective are both 3D drawing techniques.

questions.question: Vertical edges in an isometric drawing stay ____.
questions.memo: Isometric keeps verticals vertical.

questions.question: Single-point perspective differs from two-point perspective because it uses…
options: one vanishing point instead of two
questions.expected: one vanishing point instead of two
questions.memo: Single-point uses one vanishing point; two-point uses two.

questions.question: A 30° set square helps draw isometric lines.
questions.memo: A 30°/60° set square is used to draw the 30° isometric lines.

TECH.G8.DG.A3.title: Developments (nets)
TECH.G8.DG.A3.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G8 T1) — Graphics & drawing: Developments (nets).

questions.question: What is a 'development' (net) in drawing?
options: The flat shape that folds up into a 3D object
questions.expected: The flat shape that folds up into a 3D object
questions.memo: A development (net) is the flattened-out surface that folds into the 3D object.

questions.question: A development of a cube would show…
options: six connected squares that fold into a box
questions.expected: six connected squares that fold into a box
questions.memo: A cube's net is six squares joined so they fold up into the cube.

questions.question: A net is used to plan how to make packaging from a flat sheet.
questions.memo: Nets show how to cut and fold a flat sheet into a 3D container.

questions.question: Why are tabs (flaps) added to a development?
options: So the edges can be glued or joined

questions.expected: the same speed and force as the input (just reversed direction)

questions.question: Gearing 'down' trades speed for more ____.
questions.memo: Gearing down sacrifices speed to gain force.

questions.question: A clock's hands need a gear system mainly to…
options: change the speed of rotation precisely
questions.expected: change the speed of rotation precisely
questions.memo: Clock gears reduce speed precisely so hands move at the right rates.

questions.question: The output force of a gear train rises when the velocity (speed) ratio reduces the speed.
questions.memo: Reducing speed through gears raises the output force — the trade-off works both ways.

TECH.G8.MS.A4.title: Cams & cranks
TECH.G8.MS.A4.description: Mechanical Systems & Control (CAPS G8 T3) — Mechanical systems & control: Cams & cranks.
TECH.G8.MS.A4.recovery_strategy: A cam and a crank both change round motion into up-and-down (reciprocating) motion.

questions.question: What does a CAM do?
options: Changes rotary motion into up-and-down (reciprocating) motion
questions.expected: Changes rotary motion into up-and-down (reciprocating) motion
questions.memo: A cam converts rotary motion into reciprocating (up-and-down) motion of a follower.

questions.question: The part that rests on a cam and moves up and down is the…
questions.memo: The follower sits on the cam and is pushed up and down as the cam turns.

questions.question: A CRANK changes…
options: rotary motion into reciprocating motion (and back)
questions.expected: rotary motion into reciprocating motion (and back)
questions.memo: A crank converts between rotary and reciprocating motion.

questions.question: Which is an example of a crank?
questions.memo: A bicycle pedal arm is a crank turning leg push into wheel rotation.

questions.question: A cam shaped like a snail (snail cam) gives a smooth rise and a sudden drop.
questions.memo: A snail cam rises smoothly then drops sharply as it turns.

questions.question: An eccentric wheel (a circle turning off-centre) used as a cam gives…
questions.memo: An eccentric (off-centre) wheel gives a smooth, regular reciprocating motion.

questions.question: A cam turns rotary motion into ____ motion.
questions.memo: A cam produces reciprocating (back-and-forth/up-and-down) motion.

questions.question: Reciprocating motion means movement that is…
options: back and forth (or up and down) repeatedly
questions.expected: back and forth (or up and down) repeatedly
questions.memo: Reciprocating motion goes back and forth (or up and down) repeatedly.

questions.question: Cams are used in engines to open and close valves.
questions.memo: Engine camshafts use cams to push the valves open and closed.

questions.question: The part that follows the shape of a cam is called the ____.
questions.memo: The follower rides on the cam's edge and moves up and down.

questions.question: Both cams and cranks are used to…
options: change the type of motion in a machine
questions.expected: change the type of motion in a machine
questions.memo: Cams and cranks both change the type of motion (rotary↔reciprocating).

questions.question: A hand drill turned by a handle uses a crank to…
options: turn the handle's motion into rotation of the bit
questions.expected: turn the handle's motion into rotation of the bit
questions.memo: The crank handle converts hand movement into rotation of the drill bit.

questions.question: A crank is an adaptation of a second-class lever.
questions.memo: CAPS describes the crank as an adapted second-class lever.

questions.question: Sort each mechanism by what it does.
questions.expected: Valve lifters and snail cams are cams; pedal arms and drill handles are cranks.
questions.memo: Cam: rotary → reciprocating with a follower. Crank: rotary ↔ reciprocating via an arm.

questions.question: As a cam rotates once, the follower…
questions.memo: Each full turn of the cam moves the follower through one rise-and-fall cycle.

questions.question: Compared with an eccentric wheel, a snail cam gives a more sudden drop.
questions.memo: A snail cam rises gradually then drops suddenly; an eccentric gives an even motion.

questions.question: Which everyday machine uses a crank to turn rotary motion into reciprocating motion?
questions.memo: A sewing machine uses a crank to drive the needle up and down.

questions.question: An off-centre circular cam is called an ____ wheel.
questions.memo: An eccentric wheel is a circle mounted off-centre, used as a smooth cam.

questions.question: Cams and cranks are examples of mechanisms that…
options: change the direction or type of movement
questions.expected: change the direction or type of movement
questions.memo: These mechanisms change the type/direction of motion in a machine.

questions.question: A follower can be lifted by a cam and pulled back down by gravity or a spring.
questions.memo: The cam lifts the follower; gravity or a spring returns it as the cam turns.

TECH.G8.MS.A5.title: Mechanical advantage calculations
TECH.G8.MS.A5.description: Mechanical Systems & Control (CAPS G8 T3) — Mechanical systems & control: Mechanical advantage calculations.
TECH.G8.MS.A5.recovery_strategy: Mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort, worked out with simple ratios.

questions.question: Mechanical advantage (MA) is calculated as…
questions.memo: MA = load ÷ effort. An MA above 1 means a small effort moves a bigger load.

questions.question: A lever lifts a 100 N load with an effort of 25 N. The MA is…
questions.memo: MA = load ÷ effort = 100 ÷ 25 = 4.

questions.question: A lever lifts a 60 N load with a 20 N effort. The MA is…
An MA greater than 1 means the machine multiplies your effort.
questions.memo: MA > 1 means the load is bigger than the effort — the machine multiplies force.

questions.question: If MA is less than 1, the machine…
options: needs more effort than the load (but may gain speed/distance)
questions.expected: needs more effort than the load (but may gain speed/distance)
questions.memo: MA < 1 means effort exceeds load — you trade force for speed or distance (like a third-class lever).

questions.question: For gears, MA can be found from the ratio of…
questions.memo: Gear MA ≈ driven teeth ÷ driver teeth (a larger driven gear gives more force).

questions.question: A driver gear of 10 teeth turns a driven gear of 40 teeth. The force MA is about…
questions.memo: 40 ÷ 10 = 4, so the force is multiplied about 4 times.

questions.question: In Grade 8 you calculate MA using ratios, not by 'taking moments'.
questions.memo: CAPS Grade 8 uses simple ratios for MA, not the moments method.

questions.question: Mechanical advantage = load ÷ ____.
questions.memo: MA = load ÷ effort.

questions.question: A wheelbarrow lets a 30 N effort lift a 120 N load. The MA is…
A lever has an effort arm of 80 cm and a load arm of 20 cm. The MA is…
questions.memo: MA for a lever = effort arm ÷ load arm = 80 ÷ 20 = 4.

questions.question: A longer effort arm gives a bigger mechanical advantage on a lever.
questions.memo: Increasing the effort arm relative to the load arm increases MA.

questions.question: If the load and effort are equal, the MA is…
questions.memo: Equal load and effort give MA = 1 — no force multiplication.

questions.question: For gears, MA is about the driven teeth divided by the ____ teeth.
questions.memo: Gear MA ≈ driven teeth ÷ driver teeth.

questions.question: Sort each result by whether the machine multiplies force.
questions.expected: MA = load÷effort: 100/20=5 and 90/30=3 multiply force; 50/50=1 and 10/40=0.25 do not.
questions.memo: Work out load ÷ effort. Above 1 multiplies force; 1 or below does not.

questions.question: A machine with MA = 5 lifts a 200 N load. The effort needed is…
questions.memo: Effort = load ÷ MA = 200 ÷ 5 = 40 N.

questions.question: MA has no units because it is a ratio of two forces.
questions.memo: MA = force ÷ force, so the units cancel and MA is just a number.

questions.question: Gearing up for speed (large drives small) usually gives an MA that is…
questions.memo: Gearing up for speed reduces force, giving an MA below 1.

questions.question: If MA is 3 and the effort is 20 N, the load lifted is ____ N.
questions.memo: Load = MA × effort = 3 × 20 = 60 N.

questions.question: Why calculate MA before building a machine?
options: To check it can move the load with the effort available
questions.expected: To check it can move the load with the effort available
questions.memo: Calculating MA confirms the machine can do the job with the available effort.

TECH.G8.MS.A6.title: Systems diagrams
TECH.G8.MS.A6.description: Mechanical Systems & Control (CAPS G8 T3) — Mechanical systems & control: Systems diagrams.
TECH.G8.MS.A6.recovery_strategy: Every system has an input, a process and an output.

questions.question: A systems diagram breaks a system into three parts:
questions.memo: A system is modelled as input → process → output.

questions.question: In a system, the INPUT is…
options: what goes in to start the system
questions.expected: what goes in to start the system
questions.memo: The input is what enters the system (energy, material, a signal).

questions.question: In a system, the OUTPUT is…
questions.memo: The output is the result the system produces.

questions.question: In a system, the PROCESS is…
options: what happens to change the input into the output
questions.expected: what happens to change the input into the output
questions.memo: The process is the action that turns the input into the output.

questions.question: Drawing a systems diagram helps you understand how a machine works.
questions.memo: Systems diagrams break a machine into clear input-process-output parts to understand it.

questions.question: A system is modelled as input → process → ____.
questions.memo: The third part of a system is the output.

questions.question: For a bicycle, the INPUT is best described as…
questions.memo: The rider's pedalling is the input that drives the bicycle system.

questions.question: For a bicycle, the OUTPUT is best described as…
options: the rear wheel turning to move the bike
questions.expected: the rear wheel turning to move the bike
questions.memo: The output is the rear wheel turning to move the bicycle.

questions.question: In a bicycle, the chain and gears are part of the PROCESS that transfers motion.
questions.memo: The chain and gears process the input (pedalling) into the output (wheel turning).

questions.question: Analysing a machine by breaking it into input-process-output is called…
questions.memo: Breaking a machine into input-process-output is systems analysis.

questions.question: The action that turns the input into the output is the ____.
questions.memo: The process is the middle step that converts input to output.

questions.question: For an electric fan: input = electricity, process = motor spins, output =…
questions.memo: The fan's output is moving air; electricity is the input and the spinning motor is the process.

questions.question: Sort each part of an electric kettle into input, process or output.
questions.expected: Electricity is the input; the heating element is the process; hot water is the output.
questions.memo: Input = electricity; process = the element heating; output = boiled water.

questions.question: Order the flow through a simple system.
questions.memo: A system flows: input → process → output.

questions.question: A gear train with a 4:1 reduction would be drawn in a systems diagram with the process being…
options: the gears reducing speed and increasing force
questions.expected: the gears reducing speed and increasing force
questions.memo: The process box describes what the gears do: reduce speed, increase force.

questions.question: A systems diagram can describe both mechanical and electrical machines.
questions.memo: Input-process-output applies to mechanical, electrical and many other systems.

questions.question: Why is breaking a machine into a system useful for designers?
options: It makes a complex machine easier to plan and fix
questions.expected: It makes a complex machine easier to plan and fix
questions.memo: Modelling a machine as a system clarifies how to plan, build and fix it.

questions.question: For a torch: input = battery energy, process = bulb glows, output = ____.
questions.memo: A torch's output is light; the battery is the input and the glowing bulb is the process.

questions.question: Which is the correct order in a systems diagram?
questions.memo: Systems flow input → process → output, in that order.

questions.question: The output of one system can become the input of another system.
questions.memo: Systems can be chained — one system's output feeds the next system's input.

TECH.G8.ES.A1.title: Circuit components & symbols
TECH.G8.ES.A1.description: Electrical Systems & Control (CAPS G8 T4) — Electrical systems & control: Circuit components & symbols.
TECH.G8.ES.A1.recovery_strategy: Devices are input (cell), output (lamp, buzzer, motor) or control (switch).

questions.question: In a circuit, an INPUT device…
options: puts energy or a signal into the circuit, like a cell
questions.expected: puts energy or a signal into the circuit, like a cell
questions.memo: Input devices (cell, generator, solar panel) put energy/signals into the circuit.

questions.question: In a circuit, an OUTPUT device…
options: turns electricity into light, sound or movement
questions.expected: turns electricity into light, sound or movement
questions.memo: Output devices (lamp, buzzer, motor, heater) turn electricity into a useful effect.

questions.question: In a circuit, a CONTROL device…
options: switches or controls the flow of current
questions.expected: switches or controls the flow of current
questions.memo: Control devices (switches) control whether and how current flows.

questions.question: Which is an OUTPUT device?
questions.memo: A motor is an output (movement); cells, solar panels and generators are inputs.

questions.question: Which is an INPUT device?
questions.memo: A solar panel supplies energy — an input; lamps, buzzers and heaters are outputs.

questions.question: A switch is a control device that opens or closes a circuit.
questions.memo: A switch controls the circuit by opening (off) or closing (on).

questions.question: A lamp, buzzer or motor is an ____ device.
questions.memo: Lamps, buzzers and motors are output devices.

questions.question: A short circuit is dangerous because…
options: current flows the wrong, easy path and can overheat
questions.expected: current flows the wrong, easy path and can overheat
questions.memo: A short circuit lets a large current take an unintended low-resistance path, which can overheat.

questions.question: Some devices can act as input, output, process or control depending on use.
questions.memo: A device's role depends on how it is used in the circuit.

questions.question: Why use accepted symbols for circuit components?
options: So any person can read the circuit clearly
questions.expected: So any person can read the circuit clearly
questions.memo: Standard symbols make circuit diagrams universally readable.

questions.question: A cell or solar panel that supplies energy is an ____ device.
questions.memo: Energy suppliers (cell, solar panel, generator) are input devices.

questions.question: A heater turns electricity into…
questions.memo: A heater is an output that converts electricity to heat.

questions.question: Connecting the components correctly avoids short circuits.
questions.memo: Correct connections keep current on the right path and avoid short circuits.

questions.question: Sort each component as input, output or control.
questions.expected: Cells and solar panels are inputs; lamps and buzzers are outputs; a switch is control.
questions.memo: Input = supplies energy; output = gives a useful effect; control = switches the current.

questions.question: A motor is best described as a device that turns electricity into…
questions.memo: A motor converts electrical energy into movement (rotation).

questions.question: A resistor can be used to limit the current in a circuit.
questions.memo: A resistor opposes current, limiting how much flows.

questions.question: Which group lists only OUTPUT devices?
questions.memo: Lamps, buzzers, motors and heaters all turn electricity into useful effects — outputs.

questions.question: A device that controls the flow of current is a ____ device.
questions.memo: Control devices (switches) control the current flow.

questions.question: Reading a circuit diagram is easier than a photo of real parts because…
questions.memo: Standard symbols are simpler and clearer than photographs of components.

questions.question: A generator is an input device that supplies electrical energy.
questions.memo: A generator produces electrical energy — an input to the circuit.

TECH.G8.ES.A2.title: Cells & energy sources
TECH.G8.ES.A2.description: Electrical Systems & Control (CAPS G8 T4) — Electrical systems & control: Cells & energy sources.
TECH.G8.ES.A2.recovery_strategy: Cells store energy; series batteries give more voltage, parallel ones last longer.

questions.question: What is an electrochemical cell?
options: A device that makes electricity from a chemical reaction
questions.expected: A device that makes electricity from a chemical reaction
questions.memo: An electrochemical cell produces electricity from a chemical reaction (a battery is made of cells).

questions.question: Connecting cells in SERIES (one after another) increases the…
questions.memo: Cells in series add their voltages together.

questions.question: Connecting cells in PARALLEL keeps the voltage the same but…
questions.memo: Cells in parallel keep voltage the same but supply current for longer.

questions.question: A 'battery' is made up of one or more cells.
questions.memo: A battery is a combination of one or more electrochemical cells.

questions.question: A photovoltaic (solar) cell turns ____ into electricity.
questions.memo: A photovoltaic cell converts sunlight directly into electricity.

questions.question: An advantage of solar cells is that they…
questions.memo: Solar cells use free, renewable sunlight — a key advantage.

questions.question: A disadvantage of solar cells is that they…
options: do not work at night or in heavy cloud
questions.expected: do not work at night or in heavy cloud
questions.memo: Solar cells need sunlight, so they don't work at night or in heavy cloud.

questions.question: You can make a simple cell from a fruit, vegetable or salt water.
questions.memo: Fruit, vegetable and salt-water cells are simple electrochemical cells.

questions.question: Cells joined in ____ add their voltages together.
questions.memo: Series cells add voltage; parallel cells extend life.

questions.question: Three 1.5 V cells connected in series give a total voltage of…
questions.memo: 1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 4.5 V for cells in series.

questions.question: Cells in parallel are useful when you need the battery to last longer.
questions.memo: Parallel cells provide current for longer at the same voltage.

questions.question: A solar cell is also called a ____ cell.
questions.memo: Solar cells are photovoltaic cells.

questions.question: Why might a torch use cells in series?
options: To give enough voltage to light the bulb brightly
questions.expected: To give enough voltage to light the bulb brightly
questions.memo: Series cells add voltage to drive the bulb brightly.

questions.question: Sort each statement under 'Series cells' or 'Parallel cells'.

items.text: Keeps voltage the same but lasts longer
Used to supply current for longer

questions.expected: Series adds voltages (e.g. 4.5 V); parallel keeps voltage but lasts longer.
questions.memo: Series → more voltage; parallel → same voltage, longer life.

questions.question: A fruit cell works because the fruit's juice acts as…
options: an electrolyte for the chemical reaction
questions.expected: an electrolyte for the chemical reaction
questions.memo: The acidic juice is the electrolyte that lets the cell's chemical reaction make electricity.

questions.question: Solar cells are environmentally friendly because they produce no smoke while working.
questions.memo: While working, solar cells make no smoke or pollution — an environmental advantage.

questions.question: Which is an INPUT (energy source) device?
questions.memo: A cell supplies energy — an input device.

questions.question: Two 1.5 V cells in series give ____ V.
questions.memo: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V in series.

questions.question: A disadvantage of ordinary batteries is that…
options: they run flat and can pollute when thrown away
questions.expected: they run flat and can pollute when thrown away
questions.memo: Batteries run flat and contain chemicals that can pollute if not disposed of properly.

questions.question: In the GET band, circuits use batteries up to a maximum of 9 V DC.
questions.memo: Safety rule: GET circuits use batteries up to 9V DC.

TECH.G8.ES.A3.title: Generating electricity for the nation
TECH.G8.ES.A3.description: Electrical Systems & Control (CAPS G8 T4) — Electrical systems & control: Generating electricity for the nation.
TECH.G8.ES.A3.recovery_strategy: Power stations (coal, water, wind) feed the national grid through step-up and step-down transformers.

questions.question: A thermal power station makes electricity by…
options: burning fuel to make steam that spins turbines
questions.expected: burning fuel to make steam that spins turbines
questions.memo: Thermal stations heat water to steam, which spins turbines connected to generators.

questions.question: Which fuel is most used in South African thermal power stations?
questions.memo: South Africa generates most of its electricity by burning coal.

questions.question: A hydroelectric power station uses the energy of…
questions.memo: Hydroelectric stations use moving/falling water to spin turbines.

questions.question: A wind turbine generates electricity using…
questions.memo: Wind turbines use the wind to turn blades that drive a generator.

questions.question: The network that carries electricity across the country is the…
questions.memo: The national grid is the network of power lines that distributes electricity.

questions.question: A step-UP transformer is used to…
options: raise the voltage for sending power long distances
questions.expected: raise the voltage for sending power long distances
questions.memo: Step-up transformers raise voltage so power travels efficiently over long distances.

questions.question: A step-DOWN transformer is used to…
options: lower the voltage to a safe level for homes
questions.expected: lower the voltage to a safe level for homes
questions.memo: Step-down transformers reduce voltage to a safe level before it reaches homes.

questions.question: Coal power produces carbon dioxide and pollution, a disadvantage of thermal stations.
questions.memo: Burning coal releases CO2 and other pollution — a key disadvantage.

questions.question: Wind and hydroelectric power are renewable and produce little pollution while running.
questions.memo: Wind and hydro are renewable and produce little pollution during operation.

questions.question: Power stations are connected to homes through the national ____.
questions.memo: The national grid distributes electricity from stations to users.

questions.question: Mains electricity in the grid is usually carried as…
questions.memo: The grid carries alternating current (AC), which transformers can change in voltage.

questions.question: A pumped-storage scheme stores energy by…
options: pumping water uphill to release later
questions.expected: pumping water uphill to release later
questions.memo: Pumped storage pumps water uphill when demand is low, then releases it to generate later.

questions.question: A disadvantage of wind power is that it only works when the wind blows.
questions.memo: Wind power depends on the wind, so output varies and can stop on calm days.

questions.question: Sort each power source as 'Renewable' or 'Non-renewable'.
questions.expected: Wind, water and solar are renewable; coal is non-renewable.
questions.memo: Renewable sources (wind, water, sun) won't run out; coal is a finite, non-renewable fuel.

questions.question: Order how electricity reaches your home from a power station.

items.text: A step-up transformer raises the voltage
Power travels along the national grid
A step-down transformer lowers the voltage for homes

questions.memo: Generate → step up → grid → step down → home. High voltage carries power efficiently, then it is lowered for safety.

questions.question: Why is power sent at high voltage across long distances?
options: It reduces energy lost in the wires
It uses less copper for the station
It is more dangerous on purpose
questions.expected: It reduces energy lost in the wires
questions.memo: High voltage reduces current and so reduces energy lost as heat in the wires.

questions.question: Industry, schools and homes all need a reliable supply of electricity.
questions.memo: A reliable supply matters for industry (jobs), schools and homes alike.

questions.question: Nuclear power stations make heat to boil water using…
questions.memo: Nuclear stations use nuclear reactions as the heat source for steam turbines.

questions.question: A transformer that lowers voltage for safe home use is a step-____ transformer.
questions.memo: Step-down transformers lower the voltage for homes.

questions.question: A balanced view of coal power is that it is…
questions.memo: Coal is reliable and relatively cheap, but it pollutes — a balanced view weighs both.

TECH.G8.ES.A4.title: Ohm's law (qualitative) & logic gates
TECH.G8.ES.A4.description: Electrical Systems & Control (CAPS G8 T4) — Electrical systems & control: Ohm's law (qualitative) & logic gates.
TECH.G8.ES.A4.recovery_strategy: More cells means more current; AND and OR logic gates decide when a circuit switches on.

questions.question: Ohm's law (in words) says that, if resistance stays the same, more voltage gives…
questions.memo: With constant resistance, increasing voltage increases the current.

questions.question: Adding more cells in series to a lamp makes it brighter (more current).
questions.memo: More cells in series raise the voltage and current, making the lamp brighter.

questions.question: An AND logic gate gives an output ON only when…
questions.memo: An AND gate outputs ON only when ALL its inputs are ON.

questions.question: An OR logic gate gives an output ON when…
questions.memo: An OR gate outputs ON when at least one input is ON.

questions.question: Two switches in SERIES behave like which logic gate?
questions.memo: Switches in series both must be closed for current to flow — AND logic.

questions.question: Two switches in PARALLEL behave like which logic gate?
questions.memo: Switches in parallel let current flow if either is closed — OR logic.

questions.question: A truth table lists the output for every combination of inputs.
questions.memo: A truth table shows the output for each possible input combination.

questions.question: A gate that needs BOTH inputs on to give an output is an ____ gate.
questions.memo: AND gates require all inputs ON.

questions.question: A gate that gives an output if EITHER input is on is an ____ gate.
questions.memo: OR gates give an output if at least one input is ON.

questions.question: A panic alarm that should trigger if EITHER of two buttons is pressed uses…
questions.memo: Either button triggering the alarm is OR logic.

questions.question: A machine that only starts when a key is in AND the lid is closed uses…
questions.memo: Both conditions required = AND logic.

questions.question: Ohm's law in Grade 8 is treated qualitatively (no calculations).
questions.memo: Grade 8 covers Ohm's law qualitatively; calculations come in Grade 9.

questions.question: If you keep the resistance the same and lower the voltage, the current will…
questions.memo: Lower voltage with the same resistance means lower current.

questions.question: Sort each set-up by its logic.
questions.expected: Series / both-needed = AND; parallel / either-works = OR.
questions.memo: AND = series, needs all inputs on. OR = parallel, needs any input on.

questions.question: For an AND gate with inputs (1, 0), the output is…
questions.memo: An AND gate needs both inputs at 1; with (1,0) the output is 0.

questions.question: For an OR gate with inputs (1, 0), the output is…
questions.memo: An OR gate gives 1 if either input is 1; (1,0) gives 1.

questions.question: More cells (more voltage) increase current only if the resistance does not change.
questions.memo: Ohm's law links them: voltage up → current up, provided resistance is constant.

questions.question: A table showing the output for every input combination is a ____ table.
questions.memo: A truth table lists outputs for all input combinations.

questions.question: Logic gates are useful in technology because they…
options: make decisions based on input conditions
questions.expected: make decisions based on input conditions
questions.memo: Logic gates let circuits 'decide' based on whether inputs are on or off.

questions.question: An AND gate output is OFF if any one of its inputs is OFF.
questions.memo: If even one input is off, an AND gate's output is off.

TECH.G8.PR.A1.title: Materials & the environment
TECH.G8.PR.A1.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G8 T2) — Processing, society & environment: Materials & the environment.

questions.question: A 'biodegradable' material is one that…

questions.question: Many natural materials have been replaced by new or improved man-made materials.

questions.question: Why is a biodegradable shopping bag better for the environment than an ordinary plastic one?
options: It breaks down instead of lasting for years as litter

questions.question: A problem with ordinary plastic shopping bags is that they…
options: last a very long time as litter and harm wildlife
questions.expected: last a very long time as litter and harm wildlife
questions.memo: Ordinary plastic bags persist as litter for years and can harm wildlife.

questions.question: Some new materials are designed to be more environmentally friendly than the ones they replace.

questions.question: A material that rots away naturally is ____.
questions.memo: Biodegradable = breaks down naturally.

questions.question: Charging shoppers for thicker, reusable bags aims to…
options: reduce the number of bags thrown away
questions.expected: reduce the number of bags thrown away
questions.memo: Charging for bags encourages reuse and reduces waste.

questions.question: Which is an example of replacing a natural material with a new one?
options: Using plastic instead of wood for a chair
questions.expected: Using plastic instead of wood for a chair
questions.memo: Plastic replacing wood is an example of a man-made material replacing a natural one.

questions.question: Non-biodegradable plastic can stay in the environment for hundreds of years.
questions.memo: Many plastics persist for hundreds of years because they do not biodegrade.

questions.question: Plastic that does NOT break down is called ____.
questions.memo: Non-biodegradable materials do not break down naturally.

questions.question: A positive impact of new materials can be that they are…
options: stronger, lighter or more environmentally friendly
questions.expected: stronger, lighter or more environmentally friendly
questions.memo: New materials can bring benefits like strength, lightness or being eco-friendly.

questions.question: Litter from plastic harms the environment mainly by…

questions.question: Writing a report to evaluate a material helps weigh its good and bad effects.

questions.question: Choosing materials with the environment in mind is part of being a…

questions.question: A material being 'improved' can mean it is stronger or lasts longer than before.

questions.question: Which choice reduces environmental harm the most when shopping?

Taking a new plastic bag each time

questions.question: Replacing a natural material with a man-made one is common in ____ times.

questions.question: A balanced report on plastic bags should include…

questions.expected: both the benefits and the environmental problems

questions.question: Designers can choose biodegradable materials to reduce long-term pollution.
questions.memo: Choosing biodegradable materials helps reduce long-lasting pollution.

TECH.G8.PR.A2.title: Recycling & packaging design
TECH.G8.PR.A2.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G8 T2) — Processing, society & environment: Recycling & packaging design.
TECH.G8.PR.A2.recovery_strategy: Packaging protects a product; paper and plastic can be recycled into new products.

questions.question: Recycling means…
options: turning used materials into new products
questions.expected: turning used materials into new products
questions.memo: Recycling reprocesses used materials into new products.

questions.question: What is the main job of packaging?
options: To protect and contain a product
questions.expected: To protect and contain a product
questions.memo: Packaging protects, contains and helps present a product.

questions.question: Waste paper and cardboard can be recycled into new packaging products.
questions.memo: Paper and cardboard are commonly recycled into new packaging.

questions.question: Good packaging design uses…
options: just enough material to do the job
questions.expected: just enough material to do the job
questions.memo: Efficient packaging uses just enough material — protecting the product without waste.

questions.question: The nature of the product mainly decides the packaging's…
questions.memo: What the product is (fragile, heavy, food) decides the packaging design and materials.

questions.question: Turning used cardboard into new boxes is called ____.
questions.memo: Recycling reprocesses used material into new products.

questions.question: Recycling reduces the amount of waste sent to landfill.
questions.memo: Recycling keeps materials in use and out of landfill.

questions.question: Fragile packaging (for eggs or glass) needs to be…
questions.memo: Fragile goods need cushioning, protective packaging.

questions.question: A 'development' is used in packaging to…
options: plan the flat shape that folds into the box
questions.expected: plan the flat shape that folds into the box

questions.question: Using recycled materials for packaging is more environmentally friendly.

questions.question: Packaging that uses too much material is ____ for the environment.
questions.memo: Over-packaging wastes material and harms the environment.

questions.question: Which is the most environmentally friendly packaging choice?
