questions.question: Order the steps to design and make simple packaging.

items.text: Investigate the product to be packaged

questions.memo: Investigate the product, design the net, cut and fold, then assemble and test.

questions.question: Sort each material by whether it is easily recyclable.
questions.expected: Clean cardboard and paper recycle easily; mixed foam and food-soiled wrappers are hard to recycle.
questions.memo: Clean paper and cardboard recycle well; mixed materials and food-soiled items are hard to recycle.

questions.question: Packaging that is easy to open and reseal shows good…
questions.memo: Easy opening and resealing is good ergonomics — ease of use.

questions.question: Over-packaging a product wastes material and money.
questions.memo: Excess packaging wastes both material and money and harms the environment.

questions.question: Recycling paper into packaging is an example of technology with a…
options: positive impact on society and the environment
questions.expected: positive impact on society and the environment
questions.memo: Recycling paper into packaging is a positive technological impact.

questions.question: Packaging's main job is to protect and ____ a product.
questions.memo: Packaging protects and contains the product.

questions.question: Why investigate how cardboard is recycled before designing packaging?
options: So your design can be recycled too
questions.expected: So your design can be recycled too
questions.memo: Understanding recycling helps you design packaging that can also be recycled.

questions.question: Designing packaging that uses recycled material and can be recycled again is good for the planet.
questions.memo: Recycled-in and recyclable-out packaging reduces waste and resource use.

TECH.G8.PR.A3.title: Impact of technology
TECH.G8.PR.A3.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G8 T2) — Processing, society & environment: Impact of technology.
TECH.G8.PR.A3.recovery_strategy: Technology has good and bad impacts; we can design to reduce the harm.

questions.question: Technology can have…
questions.memo: Technology brings both benefits and harms, which must be weighed.

questions.question: Which is a POSITIVE impact of technology?
questions.memo: Easier communication is a positive impact of technology.

questions.question: Which is a NEGATIVE impact of technology?
questions.memo: Pollution is a negative impact of technology.

questions.question: We can sometimes design solutions to counteract the negative impact of a technology.
questions.memo: Designers can create solutions that reduce or counteract negative impacts.

questions.question: A factory pours waste into a river. A good counter-solution is to…
options: treat the waste before releasing it
questions.expected: treat the waste before releasing it
questions.memo: Treating waste before release reduces the harmful impact on the river.

questions.question: A solution that reduces a technology's harm helps to ____ its negative impact.
questions.memo: To counteract means to reduce or offset the negative impact.

questions.question: Every technology should be judged by weighing its benefits against its harms.
questions.memo: Balanced judgement weighs the benefits and harms of a technology.

questions.question: Cars give us fast transport (positive) but also cause…
questions.memo: Cars provide transport but pollute the air — a clear positive-and-negative example.

questions.question: A technological product with a negative social impact might be one that…
options: replaces many workers, causing job losses
questions.expected: replaces many workers, causing job losses
questions.memo: Automation that causes job losses is a negative social impact.

questions.question: A class discussion can help find solutions to counteract a technology's harm.
questions.memo: Discussing ideas helps find ways to reduce a technology's negative impact.

questions.question: Pollution from factories is a ____ impact of technology.
questions.memo: Pollution is a negative impact.

questions.question: Reinforcing materials or improving a product can reduce…
options: the negative effects of a technology
questions.expected: the negative effects of a technology
questions.memo: Improving or adapting a product can reduce its negative effects.

questions.question: Sort each effect of technology as positive or negative.
questions.expected: Vaccines and phones are positive; factory smoke and e-waste are negative.
questions.memo: Weigh both sides: medicine and communication help; pollution and waste harm.

questions.question: Evaluating a solution to a negative impact, you should check its…
questions.memo: A solution is evaluated for effectiveness, fairness, accuracy and scope.

questions.question: Some technologies help one part of society while harming another.
questions.memo: A technology can benefit one group while harming another — a sign to weigh carefully.

questions.question: The best response to a technology's negative impact is usually to…
options: redesign or add a solution to reduce the harm
questions.expected: redesign or add a solution to reduce the harm
questions.memo: Redesigning to reduce harm is the responsible response.

questions.question: Better medicine is a ____ impact of technology.
questions.memo: Improved medicine is a positive impact.

questions.question: Why is it important to think about impact when designing?
options: So benefits are kept and harms reduced
questions.expected: So benefits are kept and harms reduced
questions.memo: Considering impact lets designers keep the benefits while reducing harm.

questions.question: A solution that fixes one problem but creates a bigger one is not a good solution.
questions.memo: A good solution must not cause a worse problem than the one it solves.

questions.question: Recycling and pollution control are technologies that mainly aim to…
questions.memo: These technologies aim to reduce environmental harm.

TECH.G8.PR.A4.title: Mining impact, indigenous mining & bias
TECH.G8.PR.A4.description: Processing, Society & Environment (CAPS G8 T2) — Processing, society & environment: Mining impact, indigenous mining & bias.
TECH.G8.PR.A4.recovery_strategy: Mining brings wealth but harms the environment, and technology can carry bias against groups.

questions.question: South Africa is rich in mineral resources, so mining is important for…
questions.memo: Mining provides jobs and is a major part of South Africa's economy.

questions.question: A negative environmental impact of mining is…
questions.memo: Acid mine drainage pollutes water — a serious negative impact of mining.

questions.question: Dust pollution from mine dumps mainly affects…
options: the air and health of nearby residents
the colour of the sky permanently
questions.expected: the air and health of nearby residents
questions.memo: Dust from mine dumps pollutes the air and harms nearby residents' health.

questions.question: Mining can bring wealth but also harm the environment.
questions.memo: Mining brings economic benefits but has real environmental costs.

questions.question: Indigenous mining of iron in South Africa before the modern era shows that…
options: local people had their own mining technology long ago
questions.expected: local people had their own mining technology long ago
questions.memo: Indigenous communities mined and worked iron long before the modern era.

questions.question: What is 'gender bias' in career choices related to mining?
options: Unfairly favouring one gender for jobs
questions.expected: Unfairly favouring one gender for jobs
questions.memo: Gender bias unfairly favours one gender over another for opportunities.

questions.question: Bias in technology means a group can be unfairly favoured or disadvantaged.
questions.memo: Bias means unfair favouring or disadvantaging of a group.

questions.question: Acid mine ____ is polluted water that leaks from mines.
questions.memo: Acid mine drainage is acidic, polluted water from mines.

questions.question: Mining is described as dangerous because…
options: deep tunnels can collapse or have rock bursts
questions.expected: deep tunnels can collapse or have rock bursts
questions.memo: Deep mining risks rock bursts and cave-ins, making it dangerous work.

questions.question: Studying indigenous mining shows that valuable technology existed before modern times.
questions.memo: Indigenous mining is evidence of advanced local technology in the past.

questions.question: Unfairly favouring one group over another in technology is called ____.
questions.memo: Bias is unfair favouring or disadvantaging of a group.

questions.question: A fair, balanced report on mining would include…
options: both the benefits and the environmental harm
questions.expected: both the benefits and the environmental harm
questions.memo: A balanced report weighs mining's benefits and its environmental harm.

questions.question: Sort each statement about mining as a 'Benefit' or a 'Harm'.
questions.expected: Jobs and minerals are benefits; acid drainage and dust are harms.
questions.memo: Mining benefits (jobs, minerals) must be weighed against harms (water and air pollution).

questions.question: How can mining companies reduce their environmental harm?
options: Treat waste water and control dust
questions.expected: Treat waste water and control dust
questions.memo: Treating waste water and controlling dust reduces mining's harm.

questions.question: Mining affects, directly or indirectly, the lives of many people in society.
questions.memo: Mining and its industries touch the lives of many across society.

questions.question: Removing gender bias in mining careers means…
options: giving fair opportunities to all genders
questions.expected: giving fair opportunities to all genders
questions.memo: Fair opportunity for all genders removes gender bias.

questions.question: Mining brings ____ but also harms the environment.
questions.memo: Mining creates wealth but damages the environment.

questions.question: Why investigate the impact of mining as part of Technology?
options: To understand technology's effect on society and the environment
questions.expected: To understand technology's effect on society and the environment
questions.memo: Studying mining shows how technology affects society and the environment.

questions.question: Indigenous people had intellectual property in their traditional mining knowledge.
questions.memo: Traditional mining knowledge is indigenous intellectual property deserving respect.

questions.question: A responsible mining technology would aim to…
options: get minerals while protecting people and the environment
questions.expected: get minerals while protecting people and the environment
questions.memo: Responsible mining balances getting minerals with protecting people and nature.

TECH.G9.DG.A1.title: First-angle orthographic projection
TECH.G9.DG.A1.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G9 T1) — Graphics & drawing: First-angle orthographic projection.
TECH.G9.DG.A1.recovery_strategy: Orthographic projection shows an object as three flat views: front, top and side.

questions.question: Orthographic projection shows an object using…
questions.memo: Orthographic projection represents a 3D object as separate flat views.

questions.question: Which three views are normally drawn in orthographic projection?
questions.memo: The standard set is the front view, top view and side view.

questions.question: Orthographic views are drawn to scale with correct dimensions.
questions.memo: Orthographic views use a scale, correct line types and dimensions.

questions.question: The 'front view' of an object shows…
options: what you see looking straight at the front
questions.expected: what you see looking straight at the front
questions.memo: The front view is the straight-on view of the front face.

questions.question: The 'top view' (plan) shows the object…
questions.memo: The top view (plan) is what you see looking straight down.

questions.question: In first-angle projection, hidden edges are drawn with…
questions.memo: Hidden detail uses dashed lines, as in earlier grades.

questions.question: Orthographic drawings show an object as separate flat ____.
questions.memo: Orthographic projection uses separate flat views.

questions.question: Why use orthographic projection for a working drawing?
options: It shows true sizes and shapes for accurate making
questions.expected: It shows true sizes and shapes for accurate making
questions.memo: Orthographic views give true, measurable shapes for accurate manufacture.

questions.question: Different line types (solid, dashed, chain) each have a meaning in orthographic drawing.
questions.memo: Solid = visible, dashed = hidden, chain = centre lines — each has a set meaning.

questions.question: A centre line in orthographic projection is drawn as a…
questions.memo: Centre lines use the chain (dash-dot) line.

questions.question: The view from directly above is the ____ view (plan).
questions.memo: The top view is the plan, seen from above.

questions.question: If a plan will NOT actually solve the problem, the drawing should be…
options: penalised, even if it is neat
questions.expected: penalised, even if it is neat
questions.memo: CAPS stresses the plan must work — a neat but non-working plan is penalised.

questions.question: Orthographic projection is useful for showing the exact measurements of a part.
questions.memo: Because views are flat and to scale, exact measurements can be shown and read.

questions.question: A simple cube drawn in orthographic projection would have a front, top and side view that are all…
questions.memo: Every orthographic view of a cube is a square.

questions.question: The main difference between orthographic and isometric drawing is that orthographic shows…
options: flat separate views, not a single 3D picture
questions.expected: flat separate views, not a single 3D picture
questions.memo: Orthographic gives flat separate views; isometric gives one 3D picture.

questions.question: Working drawings in Grade 9 use first-angle ____ projection.
questions.memo: Grade 9 working drawings use first-angle orthographic projection.

TECH.G9.DG.A2.title: Working drawings & design problems
TECH.G9.DG.A2.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G9 T1) — Graphics & drawing: Working drawings & design problems.
TECH.G9.DG.A2.recovery_strategy: A working drawing must really solve the problem — neat is not enough if it won't work.

questions.question: The most important thing about a working drawing of a solution is that…
questions.memo: A working drawing must show a solution that genuinely solves the problem.

questions.question: A wheelchair ramp design must have a gentle enough…
questions.memo: A ramp's gradient must be gentle enough for a wheelchair to use safely.

questions.question: A design brief for a stair should state the number of steps and the riser height.
questions.memo: The brief specifies details like number of steps, riser height and ramp gradient.

questions.question: The 'riser' of a stair is the…
questions.memo: The riser is the vertical face/height of each step.

questions.question: A working drawing should be drawn…
questions.memo: Working drawings are to scale with correct dimensions and line types.

questions.question: Even a very neat plan should be marked down if it would not actually solve the problem.
questions.memo: CAPS is clear: a plan that won't work must be penalised, however neat.

questions.question: A ramp that is too steep is NOT ____-for-purpose for a wheelchair.
questions.memo: Too steep means it fails fitness-for-purpose for a wheelchair user.

questions.question: Why add a handrail to a stair or ramp design?
options: For safety and support of users
questions.expected: For safety and support of users
questions.memo: A handrail improves safety and gives users support.

questions.question: A flow chart in the design process shows…
options: the order of steps to make the solution
questions.expected: the order of steps to make the solution
questions.memo: A flow chart sets out the sequence of manufacturing steps.

questions.question: A working drawing helps the maker build the solution accurately.
questions.memo: Accurate, dimensioned working drawings guide accurate making.

questions.question: The flat part of a step you stand on is the ____.
questions.memo: The tread is the horizontal part of a step; the riser is the vertical part.

questions.question: If a wheelchair ramp design is drawn too steep, the correct response is to…
options: redesign it with a gentler slope
leave it because it is neat
questions.expected: redesign it with a gentler slope
questions.memo: A too-steep ramp must be redesigned to a usable, gentler slope.

questions.question: A good design solution balances being workable, safe and…
questions.memo: Solutions should be workable, safe and affordable (cost-effective).

questions.question: Specifications in a design brief give measurable requirements the design must meet.
questions.memo: Specifications state measurable requirements (sizes, gradient, materials).

questions.question: A working drawing for a stair should include…
options: dimensions, scale and correct line types
only a sketch with no sizes
questions.expected: dimensions, scale and correct line types
questions.memo: It needs dimensions, a scale and correct line conventions to be built from.

questions.question: A plan must, above all, actually ____ the problem.
questions.memo: The plan must solve the problem — that is the top priority.

TECH.G9.DG.A3.title: Artistic & exploded assembly drawing
TECH.G9.DG.A3.description: Design Process & Graphics (CAPS G9 T1) — Graphics & drawing: Artistic & exploded assembly drawing.
TECH.G9.DG.A3.recovery_strategy: An exploded view shows the parts pulled apart to reveal how they fit together.

questions.question: An 'exploded' assembly drawing shows the parts…
options: separated but lined up to show how they fit together
questions.expected: separated but lined up to show how they fit together
questions.memo: An exploded view separates the parts along their assembly lines to show how they fit.

questions.question: An artistic impression is mainly used to…
options: show how the finished product will look
questions.expected: show how the finished product will look
questions.memo: Artistic impressions communicate the look of the finished product.

questions.question: Single vanishing point perspective can be used to draw a realistic 3D object.
questions.memo: Single-point perspective gives a realistic 3D impression.

questions.question: Adding wood-grain texture, colour and shadows to a drawing makes it…
questions.memo: Texture, colour and shadows enhance realism in an artistic drawing.

questions.question: An exploded view is most useful for showing…
options: how to assemble a product from its parts
questions.expected: how to assemble a product from its parts
questions.memo: Exploded views show assembly order and how parts connect.

questions.question: A drawing that separates parts to show how they fit is an ____ view.
questions.memo: An exploded view separates and aligns the parts.

questions.question: Artistic drawings are usually used to communicate, not to give building measurements.
questions.memo: Artistic impressions communicate appearance; working drawings give the measurements.

questions.question: Shadows added to a perspective drawing help to show…
questions.memo: Shadows give a sense of depth and three-dimensional form.

questions.question: Which drawing would best show a customer the final look of a product?
questions.memo: An artistic perspective impression best shows the final appearance.

questions.question: An exploded view usually keeps the parts in line along the direction they fit together.
questions.memo: Parts in an exploded view stay aligned along their assembly axes.

questions.question: Single ____ point perspective uses one point where lines meet in the distance.
questions.memo: Single vanishing point perspective uses one vanishing point.

questions.question: Why might a designer include an exploded view in a presentation?
options: To show clearly how the product is put together
questions.expected: To show clearly how the product is put together
questions.memo: Exploded views clearly communicate how a product assembles.

questions.question: Texture in a drawing can show whether a surface is wood, metal or rough.
questions.memo: Drawn texture suggests the material and surface finish (wood grain, metal sheen).

questions.question: Artistic and exploded drawings are both mainly about…
questions.memo: Both communicate the design — its look and how it fits together.

questions.question: Compared with an orthographic drawing, an exploded 3D view is better at showing…
questions.memo: Exploded 3D views show relationships and assembly; orthographic gives flat measurements.

questions.question: Colour, texture and ____ make an artistic drawing look realistic.
questions.memo: Shadows (with colour and texture) add realism.

TECH.G9.ST.A1.title: Forces: static, dynamic & loads
TECH.G9.ST.A1.description: Structures (CAPS G9 T1) — Structures: Forces: static, dynamic & loads.
TECH.G9.ST.A1.recovery_strategy: Forces can be static (still) or dynamic (moving); loads can be even or uneven.

questions.question: A STATIC force is one that…
options: stays still or steady, like a parked car's weight
questions.expected: stays still or steady, like a parked car's weight
questions.memo: A static force is steady and unchanging, like the weight of a stationary object.

questions.question: A DYNAMIC force is one that…
options: changes or moves, like wind gusts or traffic
questions.expected: changes or moves, like wind gusts or traffic
questions.memo: A dynamic force changes or moves, like wind, waves or moving traffic.

questions.question: An EVEN (uniform) load is spread…
questions.memo: An even load is distributed evenly across the structure.

questions.question: An UNEVEN (point) load acts…
questions.memo: An uneven (point) load concentrates at one place.

questions.question: The weight of people walking on a bridge is a dynamic load.
questions.memo: Moving people create a changing, dynamic load on a bridge.

questions.question: A heavy statue standing still on a plinth applies a static load.
questions.memo: A still statue's steady weight is a static load.

questions.question: A force that changes or moves is a ____ force.
questions.memo: Dynamic forces change or move; static forces are steady.

questions.question: Internal cross-bracing helps a structure resist…
questions.memo: Cross-bracing resists twisting and racking by triangulating the frame.

questions.question: Wind blowing in gusts against a building is an example of a…
questions.memo: Gusting wind is a changing, dynamic load.

questions.question: A load spread evenly over a structure is an ____ load.
questions.memo: An even load is distributed uniformly.

questions.question: Designers must consider both static and dynamic forces when designing a structure.
questions.memo: Real structures face both steady (static) and changing (dynamic) forces.

questions.question: A bookshelf loaded with books all along it carries mainly a…
questions.memo: Books spread along the shelf give an even, distributed load.

questions.question: A person standing on one spot of a plank applies a…
questions.memo: Weight at one spot is a point (uneven) load.

questions.question: Sort each force/load as static or dynamic.

items.text: Weight of a parked car on a slab

questions.expected: Steady weights are static; moving wind and traffic are dynamic.
questions.memo: Static = steady/unchanging; dynamic = moving/changing.

questions.question: Why are dynamic loads often harder on a structure than static ones?
options: Changing forces can cause vibration and fatigue
questions.expected: Changing forces can cause vibration and fatigue
questions.memo: Dynamic loads change and can cause vibration and fatigue, stressing a structure.

questions.question: Torsion is a twisting force that structures may need to resist.
questions.memo: Torsion (twisting) is one of the forces a structure may have to resist.

questions.question: A single concentrated load at one place is a ____ load.
questions.memo: A point load is concentrated at one place.

questions.question: A crane lifting different weights through the day puts a ____ load on its structure.
questions.memo: Changing lifted weights create a dynamic load.

questions.question: An even load is generally easier for a structure to carry than the same total weight at one point.
questions.memo: Spreading the load reduces concentrated stress, so an even load is usually easier to carry.

questions.question: Why consider the type of load before choosing a material?
options: So the material and shape can resist that load
questions.expected: So the material and shape can resist that load
questions.memo: Knowing the load lets you choose a material/shape that can resist it.

TECH.G9.ST.A2.title: Strength of materials & cross-sections
TECH.G9.ST.A2.description: Structures (CAPS G9 T1) — Structures: Strength of materials & cross-sections.
TECH.G9.ST.A2.recovery_strategy: A material's cross-section, like an I-beam, helps it resist bending without extra weight.

questions.question: Why is a steel I-beam shaped like an 'I'?
options: The shape resists bending while saving material
questions.expected: The shape resists bending while saving material
questions.memo: The I-shape puts material where bending stress is greatest, saving weight.

questions.question: A hollow tube can be strong and stiff while being…
questions.memo: A tube's cross-section gives strength and stiffness for little weight.

questions.question: 'Angle iron' (an L-shaped section) is used because the shape…
options: resists bending better than a flat strip
questions.expected: resists bending better than a flat strip
questions.memo: The L-shaped cross-section stiffens the section against bending.

questions.question: Changing the cross-section of a member can make it stronger without adding much weight.
questions.memo: The right cross-section (I, tube, L) adds stiffness efficiently.

questions.question: Which force stretches a material?
questions.memo: Tension is a pulling/stretching force.

questions.question: Which force squashes a material?
questions.memo: Compression squashes; tension stretches.

questions.question: Internal cross-bracing helps a member resist twisting (torsion).
questions.memo: Cross-bracing inside a member resists torsion (twisting).

questions.question: An I-shaped beam is also called a ____.
questions.memo: A large I-beam is commonly called a girder.

questions.question: A T-bar or I-beam is chosen partly to…
options: use as much metal as possible
questions.memo: These sections resist forces efficiently, saving material.

questions.question: A bending beam is squashed on one side and stretched on the other, meaning it has…
questions.memo: Bending creates compression on one face and tension on the other.

questions.question: A round tube resists bending in all directions roughly equally.
questions.memo: A circular cross-section resists bending evenly in all directions.

questions.question: Putting material where bending is greatest, like in an ____-beam, saves weight.
questions.memo: The I-beam puts material in the top and bottom flanges where bending stress is highest.

questions.question: Which would be the strongest against bending for the same amount of steel?
questions.memo: An I-beam uses the steel most efficiently to resist bending.

questions.question: Sort each section/use by the main reason it is chosen.

items.text: Hollow tube instead of solid bar
Thin-walled tube for a light frame

questions.expected: I-beams and angle iron add stiffness; hollow/thin tubes save weight while staying strong.
questions.memo: Cross-sections are chosen both to add stiffness (I-beam, angle) and to save material (tubes).

questions.question: Reinforced concrete adds steel because concrete is weak in…
questions.memo: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel is added for tensile strength.

questions.question: Choosing the right cross-section is part of designing a strong, efficient structure.
questions.memo: Cross-section choice is key to strong, material-efficient design.

questions.question: A bicycle frame uses tubes rather than solid rods mainly to be…
questions.memo: Tubes give the strength and stiffness needed while keeping the frame light.

questions.question: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in ____.
questions.memo: Concrete handles compression well but is weak in tension.

questions.question: The cross-section of a member is…
options: the shape you see when you cut straight through it
questions.expected: the shape you see when you cut straight through it

questions.question: The best of the three Rs to do first is 'reduce', because using less avoids waste entirely.
questions.memo: Reducing comes first — using less avoids creating the waste at all.

questions.question: Turning used plastic into new products is called ____.
questions.memo: Recycling reprocesses used plastic into new products.

questions.question: Cutting, bending and joining plastic are skills used to…
questions.memo: Measuring, cutting, bending and joining are how a plastic item is made.

questions.question: Order the steps to recycle plastic into a new product.

items.text: Shred and melt it into pellets
Mould the pellets into a new product

questions.memo: Collect and sort, shred/melt into pellets, mould into a new product, then use it.

questions.question: Sort each action under the correct 'R'.

items.text: Buy a drink in a refillable bottle
Use an old jar to store screws
Send plastic bottles to be made into pellets

questions.expected: Refillable bottles and less packaging reduce; reusing a jar is reuse; sending bottles for pellets is recycling.
questions.memo: Reduce = use less; reuse = use again; recycle = reprocess into something new.

questions.question: Remanufacturing waste plastic into pellets is valuable because it…
options: turns waste into a useful raw material
questions.expected: turns waste into a useful raw material
questions.memo: Pelletising turns waste plastic into a reusable raw material.

questions.question: Recycling helps reduce the amount of plastic litter in the environment.
questions.memo: Recycling keeps plastic in use and out of the environment as litter.

questions.question: A plastics recycling project is best described in a systems diagram as…
questions.memo: Recycling fits input-process-output: waste in, processing, new product out.

questions.question: Using an item again instead of discarding it is to ____ it.
questions.memo: Reuse means using the same item again.

questions.question: Why is recycling plastic better than sending it to landfill?
options: It saves resources and reduces pollution
questions.expected: It saves resources and reduces pollution
questions.memo: Recycling saves raw materials and cuts pollution compared with landfill.

questions.question: Choosing products with less packaging is an example of 'reduce'.
questions.memo: Less packaging means less waste created — that is reducing.
